The learned gates turn low-pass on their own and make the scan far less sensitive to how the matches are shuffled. Together, these results show that frequency is a natural language for describing agreement between correspondences, with implications for other sequence models that must read unordered sets, such as point clouds and graphs.

authors.name: Zhihua Wang, Yifeng Gao, Yunhao Feng, Rui Pan, Zhouyuan Ma, Baiheng Zhao, Zixing Chen, Yanping Li, Yizhang Liu, Xingjun Ma

papers.title: ICA Lens: Non-Gaussianity Reveals Interpretable Directions in Language Models
papers.summary: Finding human-interpretable directions in language-model activations is important for understanding and controlling model behavior. These directions are usually discovered through indirect learning objectives such as sparse reconstruction, but it remains unclear what existing statistical structure distinguishes interpretable directions and whether that structure can be used directly for feature discovery. We find that non-Gaussianity provides such a signature: projection distributions of natural-text residual-stream activations along sparse autoencoder (SAE) decoder directions are substantially more non-Gaussian than those along random directions, with most contexts forming a concentrated background and recurring patterns often occupying one tail. This raises a natural question: if interpretable directions tend to have non-Gaussian projection distributions, can we discover them by searching for non-Gaussian directions directly in activation space, without training another sparse dictionary? To test this hypothesis, we introduce ICA Lens, a practical workflow for efficient discovery, reliable annotation, and faithful evaluation of non-Gaussian directions in LLM residual-stream activations. Across GPT-2 Small, Gemma 2 2B, and Qwen 3.5 9B Base, we find that (1) the recovered non-Gaussian directions capture coherent lexical, syntactic, and semantic patterns under both human and LLM-based evaluation; (2) non-Gaussianity is positively associated with both human-label confidence and automated interpretability; and (3) the resulting coordinates are competitive with SAEs across interpretability, sparse reconstruction, concept prediction, and causal interventions, while fitting in minutes per layer and using 7-43 times less memory. These results show that non-Gaussianity is a direct unsupervised signal for discovering interpretable and useful structure in activations.

authors.name: Sida Liu, Feijiang Han, Sarah Wiegreffe, Furong Huang

papers.title: FoundCause: A Foundation Model for Causal Discovery with Latent Confounders from Observational Data
papers.summary: Causal discovery from observational data requires recovering directed relations and latent confounding without interventions. We propose FoundCause, an {\em amortized causal discovery foundation model} trained only on synthetic structural causal models that maps datasets to causal graphs in a single forward pass. A permutation-equivariant transformer alternates attention over samples and variables to model cross-variable dependence and per-variable distributions. Pairwise dependence and asymmetry statistics guide its attention, edge decoder and confounder module. The decoder separates edge existence from direction, while triangular refinement incorporates evidence from chains and colliders. Learnable latent tokens predict which variable pairs share a hidden common cause, and a masked input representation handles missing data. To our knowledge, FoundCause is the first amortized causal discovery approach for i.i.d. observational data to predict latent confounding as a separate, explicit output. On 14 real-world and semi-synthetic datasets, FoundCause leads 11 classical and 7 amortized baselines in average AUROC, $F_1$, skeleton $F_1$, and normalized structural Hamming distance ($\mathrm{SHD}/d$): clearly in $\mathrm{SHD}/d$ ($0.875$ vs.\ $0.956$), narrowly in $F_1$ ($0.531$ vs.\ $0.516$). It also has the highest accuracy among amortized methods on bivariate cause--effect pairs.

authors.name: Patrick Bl\"obaum, Krishnakumar Balasubramanian, Shiva Prasad Kasiviswanathan

papers.title: Offline Preference-Based Trajectory Evaluation
papers.summary: Offline evaluation of agentic systems often collapses trajectories into a binary terminal success value, discarding information about partial progress. This, in turn, results in widespread ties that create statistical inefficiency by reducing effective sample size and weakening the ability to distinguish systems. We propose preference-based trajectory evaluation, an evaluation measure that compares pairs of trajectories directly by using temporal preferences between time-to-return profiles. We find that, across diverse agentic and interactive benchmarks, success-based metrics result in tied comparisons on roughly 75% of instances, while trajectory-aware preferences reduce ties to roughly 35%, improving discriminative power, ranking stability, and data efficiency. Our results suggest that benchmark saturation, often portrayed as the result of poor data collection or problem difficulty, may also be explained by the design of the evaluation measure.

authors.name: Fernando Diaz

papers.title: The Language-Energy Divide: Measuring Energy Costs of Multilingual LLM Inference
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multilingual settings, yet the energy costs of serving these models across different languages remain poorly understood. We present a systematic study of inference energy consumption across languages with ML.Energy framework (Chung et al., 2026). We find striking disparities: energy consumption per output token varies by up to 8.3 times across languages, while total energy for a fixed set of requests varies by up to 179 times between the cheapest (English, 17.6 kJ) and the most expensive (Pashto, 3,147 kJ) languages. Our analysis shows that this disparity is driven by two compounding factors: (1) higher per-token energy costs for languages using complex or rare scripts, and (2) more tokens generated for low-resource languages. Moreover, we find a double cost + performance penalty: languages with the highest energy footprints also tend to achieve the lowest task accuracy. We reveal that the energy divide persists across models, hardware, and tasks, suggesting a systemic energy inequity in multilingual LLM deployment. Finally, we recommend that the community treat energy as a first-class evaluation axis, extend reporting checklists and model cards to include it, and adopt deployment-side mitigations for better energy efficiency.

authors.name: Naihao Deng, Alissa Shen, Yiming Feng, Joan Nwatu, Jae-Won Chung, Mosharaf Chowdhury, Yulong Chen, Rada Mihalcea

papers.title: Spatiotemporal and Multi-Robot Motion Planning on Graphs of Space-Time Convex Sets
papers.summary: Decoupled multi-robot motion planning avoids the high-dimensional joint configuration space but requires repeated single-robot planning among moving obstacles, where route choice and timing are coupled. We develop a framework based on graphs of space-time convex sets (ST-GCSs) for continuous spatiotemporal planning and multi-robot coordination. An ST-GCS represents collision-free space-time by convex sets, allowing the sequence of regions and the geometry and timing of piecewise-linear trajectories to be optimized jointly under velocity limits. To incorporate moving obstacles and previously planned robots, we develop Exact Convex Decomposition (ECD), which removes their swept occupancies while maintaining a convex decomposition for subsequent planning queries. Building on path-based GCS search, we develop a best-first solver tailored to the ST-GCS motion model, exploiting temporal reachability for dominance pruning and using admissible heuristics with separate or joint search-key evaluation. Precomputed heuristic bounds can also be reused across reservation-updated graphs. We integrate ST-GCS planning and ECD into prioritized multi-robot planning and introduce windowed coordination with dynamic window adjustment to limit reservation-induced graph growth. Experiments demonstrate improved scalability and competitive solution quality against optimization-based and sampling-based planners on challenging spatiotemporal and multi-robot problems. Large-scale simulations coordinate up to $100$ robots within a minute, while real-robot demonstrations showcase the practical applicability of the framework. Project homepage: https://sites.google.com/view/stgcs.

authors.name: Jingtao Tang, Zining Mao, Lufan Yang, Hang Ma

papers.title: Localized LoRA-MoE: Mixture of Low-Rank Experts With Adaptive Routing
papers.summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods such as LoRA adapt large models through a single low-rank update. Such updates are susceptible to gradient interference: when a training stream interleaves multiple operational contexts, conflicting updates to shared adapter weights collapse the adapter into an unspecialized average. While recent methods introduce block-wise isolation to remedy this issue, their topologies are static and cannot adapt to context switching or localized sensor degradation. In this work, we introduce Localized LoRA-MoE, a framework that combines localized spatial blocking with context-conditioned expert routing. We propose and evaluate two architectural variants: Block-Wise LoRA-MoE (centralized routing), which modulates the entire structural grid through a single context-conditioned gate, and Cell-Wise LoRA-MoE (decentralized routing), which assigns an independent gate to every coordinate cell of the matrix grid. Across three structured transformation benchmarks--a high-dimensional SVD matrix simulation, context-switched transformations over real tabular data, and spatial reconstruction under simulated sensor occlusion--both variants outperform static baselines under comparable adapter budgets. Both variants perform similarly when context shifts the grid uniformly, while cell-wise routing is strictly better when contexts are spatially heterogeneous. When fine-tuning a language model on six interleaved GLUE tasks, task-conditioned routing at a fixed adapter budget outperforms LoRA and static localized adapters, matching per-task adapters with 6x budgets. At decoder scale on Qwen2.5-1.5B, both routed variants outperform static baselines across eight commonsense benchmarks, with cell-wise routing achieving +3.9 points over LoRA at matched active capacity.

authors.name: Babak Barazandeh, Subhabrata Majumdar, Vinay Prithyani, George Michailidis

papers.title: Statistical Adversaries: Natural Backdoor-like Adversarial Features in Clean Vision Datasets
papers.summary: Model-specific adversarial attacks have been extensively studied. We study a different failure mode: naturally occurring statistical signals in vision data that can behave as backdoor-like triggers without being maliciously inserted. We call these signals statistical adversaries. We analyse ImageNet to find patterns that are strongly linked to certain labels. We then use statistical controls to remove random correlations from our candidate signals. Finally, we demonstrate that these signals directly and predictably alter model predictions. These statistical adversaries are more targeted than generic corruptions and transfer across different model architectures. This suggests that some vulnerabilities are driven by dataset structure and distribution rather than a single model's idiosyncrasies. We conclude that ordinary datasets can contain exploitable adversarial surfaces even in the absence of poisoning, and suggest that dataset audits should treat spurious structure not only as a source of bias or interpretability failure, but also as a latent attack surface for vision models.

authors.name: Paul K. Mandal, Pavan Reddy, Tristan Malaty\'nski

papers.title: Real-time fall detection based on vision for low-power edge platforms
papers.summary: Falling detection is vital for elderly care and intelligent surveillance; however, prevailing vision-based approaches predominantly frame it as static pose classification or discrete temporal pattern matching, fundamentally overlooking the instability dynamics of the human support system. This paper proposes a physics-informed falling detection framework that recasts falling as a stability-loss event in a coupled dynamical system. We introduce a novel dual-LTC architecture comprising a Center-of-Mass (CoM) subsystem and a Base-of-Support (BoS) subsystem, both instantiated as Liquid Time-Constant (LTC) neural networks to continuously model inertial trajectory evolution and ground-contact adjustment through adaptive time constants, Physical interpretability of falling motion. A learnable coupling module emulates physical interaction between the two subsystems, while a Stability Manifold classifier operates in the joint latent space to detect boundary crossing via Lyapunov-inspired stability metrics. Complementary counterfactual trajectory projection and Time-to-Collision (TTC) estimation further enable irreversibility assessment and early warning. The architecture is designed to support a three-state prediction paradigm (Normal, Falling, Fallen); in this preliminary study, we validate the core stability discrimination capability on a two-class dataset (Normal vs. Falling), leaving the full three-state temporal transition to future work. Unlike conventional CNN--RNN pipelines, the proposed formulation encodes continuous-time mechanical inertia, yielding a sub-50K-parameter network capable of real-time inference on resource-constrained edge devices. Extensive experiments demonstrate competitive accuracy with superior physical interpretability, validating its efficacy for low-compute visual fall detection.

authors.name: Wenjun Xia, Zhicheng Peng, Haopeng Li, Zhengdi Zhang

papers.title: Adapting Generalist Vehicle Models for High-Speed MPC Across Terrains
papers.summary: High-speed off-road autonomy requires precise closed-loop control for a target vehicle while remaining robust across changing terrains. Recent forward kinodynamic (FKD) prediction foundation models suggest a promising path, starting from a generalist model and specializing it to the target platform. However, effective specialization remains challenging, as it often requires substantial real-world data, and models adapted to one setting can still overfit to specific terrains or driving regimes. We present OptCar (Optimized Car), a recipe for bridging the gap from generalist to specialist FKD models that preserves cross-terrain generalization while optimizing performance for a specific vehicle. OptCar introduces a transformer FKD architecture that uses FiLM to condition multi-step predictions on a single dynamics context token summarizing recent state-action history. It then specializes the generalist model using limited real-world data and targeted synthetic rollouts from environment-specific system identification. In closed-loop model predictive control (MPC) experiments across three terrains and an out-of-distribution cart-pulling task, the largest gains appear at 6 m/s, the highest speed evaluated and the regime in which slip dominates tracking error. On vegetation + dirt, the most slip-diverse terrain, OptCar reduces 6 m/s trajectory tracking error by roughly 55% relative to AnyCar fine-tuned on real data alone, and remains the most accurate even when an unseen cart payload changes the dynamics. With 5 minutes of real data per terrain, OptCar is competitive on road with a specialist trained on 30 minutes of road data and outperforms it when the terrain changes. Project Page : https://amrl.cs.utexas.edu/optcar/

authors.name: Rwik Rana, Jesse Quattrociocchi, Christian Ellis, Nathan Tsoi, Garrett Warnell, Joydeep Biswas

papers.title: OpenMHC: Accelerating the Science of Wearable Foundation Models
papers.summary: Mobile and wearable devices offer an unprecedented opportunity for continuous, passive health monitoring and active health coaching. However, the largest wearable datasets are proprietary, and leading wearable foundation models trained on them are rarely open weight or include reproducible training code. To accelerate open science in wearable health, we introduce OpenMyHeartCounts (OpenMHC), the largest and most comprehensive wearable health dataset broadly accessible to qualified researchers, alongside open-source implementations and weights for recent wearable foundation models. Derived from over a decade of data collected through the My Heart Counts study app, OpenMHC comprises over 67M participant-hours of wearable recordings across up to 19 sensor channels (e.g., step count, heart rate, sleep, workouts) and up to 170 health, lifestyle, mood, and behavioral variables from 11,894 participants. Furthermore, we establish a benchmark for standardized evaluation across three tasks: (1) health and behavioral outcome prediction, (2) multivariate data imputation, and (3) time-series forecasting. Benchmarking classical methods alongside recent wearable and time-series foundation models, we find that while foundation models perform strongly, carefully tuned classical baselines like XGBoost remain highly competitive. By uniting broad-access wearable data with open code and model weights, OpenMHC provides a framework needed to drive reproducible advances in wearable health AI.

authors.name: Narayan Schuetz, Yuze Bai, Lianggang Pan, Edgar Eggert, Favour Nerrise, Juan Delgado-SanMartin, Max Rosenblattl, Milana Gurbanova, Mohammad Asadi, Anders Johnson, Steven G. Hershman, Paul Schmiedmayer, Dennis Wang, Allan Lawrie, Daniel Seung Kim, Xin Liu, Akshay Paruchuri, Ehsan Adeli, Euan A. Ashley, Kelly W. Zhang

papers.title: Where Is the Cost of Third-Party API Routers in Agentic Software Development?
papers.summary: Third-party API routers have become a common layer that unifies access across increasingly diverse LLM providers. In coding-agent workflows, high-autonomy operation is widely adopted because it reduces interaction overhead. As a result, a third-party API router, which sits between the agent and the upstream provider, inevitably occupies the trusted path. It can inspect and modify every request and response, yet no mechanism verifies alignment between the provider's output and the repository-level actions ultimately executed by the agent. Consequently, client-side permission mechanisms may become ineffective in practice. Whether this control gap produces real, hard-to-detect effects on software development tasks remains empirically unmeasured. In this paper, we conduct an empirical study of router-side injection in coding agents, examining four intervention levels of increasing subtlety: Response Substitution (L1), Response Append (L2), LLM-Polished Injection (L3), and LLM-Polished with Distribution Alignment Injection (L4). Moreover, we develop SIDEL, a framework for trace recording, replay, injection, and defense evaluation, with a curated dataset of 400 samples. We evaluate four representative coding agents, and further evaluate whitelist-based execution control and LLM review. Router-side intervention substantially alters repository-level actions and remains difficult for existing client-side safeguards to detect. Without additional mitigations, all evaluated agents achieved a defense success rate of 0 percent across all injection levels. Client-side mitigations and reactive reviews improve resistance but do not fully restore end-to-end control, motivating provider-side output-integrity guarantees. Our code is available at https://github.com/Riyasushin/SIDEL.

authors.name: Donghao Fu, Jingxin Li, Xue Jiang, Yihong Dong

papers.title: LLM Misuse Safeguards Rely on Untrusted Input: A Widespread, High-Risk Vulnerability
papers.summary: Large language models now help professionals in fields such as cybersecurity and biology, yet the same answers would help an attacker. Deployers rely on misuse safeguards to keep such answers from attackers. We find that these safeguards share a high-risk vulnerability: they decide whether to release an answer from what users write, including the professional identity or purpose they claim, and anyone can write such a claim. Threat reports from model vendors and security firms show that attackers who fabricate a professional identity or purpose already exploit this vulnerability to cause serious harm. The vulnerability is also widespread across the state of the art: every defense proposed in 129 papers from the latest editions of 12 top venues has it. Safeguard research studies the wrong object: it treats harm as a property of the text of a request, although the same text can come from a professional or an attacker. Current safeguard benchmarks therefore cannot reveal the vulnerability: a safeguard can score high on them and still give dangerous answers to attackers. Because the vulnerability lies in what users write, no improvement in how safeguards judge that writing can close it. Under the patch we propose, large language models can help professionals without giving dangerous capabilities to anyone who merely claims to be one.

authors.name: Pingyu Wu, Weiming Zhang, Nenghai Yu

papers.title: RecHarness: A Bandit-Routed Agentic Harness for Self-Evolving Recommender Systems
papers.summary: Optimizing recommender models remains heavily reliant on manual iteration over architectures, objectives, and training strategies. While LLM-based agents can automate this trial-and-error process, relying on LLMs to both select modification directions and formulate concrete hypotheses can lead to unstable search under limited trial budgets. Inspired by the above challenge, we propose RecHarness, a Bandit-Routed Agentic Harness for automated recommender model optimization. RecHarness decouples the optimization process into two steps: a bandit router selects the next modification direction according to historical validation feedback, while the LLM generates a concrete optimization hypothesis and executable code edit within the selected direction. To sustain long-horizon exploration, RecHarness uses a jump-basin mechanism to activate a structural-jump arm when local edits stagnate. Across multiple recommendation tasks, datasets, and model backbones, RecHarness achieves more consistent performance improvements and uses limited trial budgets more effectively than LLM-directed search. During a 7-day online A/B test on a large-scale short-video advertising platform, the selected candidate improves ADVV by 2.084%, Revenue by 0.534%, and Exposure by 0.559%. Code is available at: https://github.com/6lyc/RecHarness.

authors.name: Haoran Ling, Yuecheng Li, Zeyu Song, Jing Yao, Shuwen Kang, Songcheng Ren, Chi Lu, Wenjin Wu, Peng Jiang

papers.title: Role Steering of Language Models for Social Simulations
papers.summary: Social simulations built from language-model agents need role-conditioned behavior that can be checked before agents are placed into a simulated population. We introduce an activation-steering screening workflow for role-conditioned agents: define a role profile, extract a role-specific direction, sweep four steering coefficients, evaluate role-profile alignment, and pass or flag each candidate configuration. On OLMo-3-7B-Instruct, we apply the workflow to a mixed 275-role inventory with 228 role-agnostic questions, GPT-4.1-mini prompted role references, and GPT-4.1-mini judges. We also introduce CastVectors, which receive higher judged role-profile alignment than an assistant-axis directional control from prior persona-vector work, with mean overall scores of 63.2 versus 41.1 across the tested grid. They also preserve high lexical diversity, while the control drops sharply at larger coefficients. The role-level screen is the main contribution: most roles improve as steering increases, but 38 roles decline across all six measured dimensions, showing why simulation builders should choose coefficients per role rather than deploy a uniform high-strength setting. Our code is available at https://github.com/HCAI-Lab-GT/casting-call-vectors, and the role vectors and evaluation data at https://huggingface.co/datasets/HCAI-Lab-GT/casting-call-vectors.

authors.name: Isaac Song, Mohammed Rehan Parwani, Glenn Matlin, Emile Anand, Akhil Theerthala, Arjun Chatterjee, Anthony Wen-Ming Zang, Maria Kostylew, Yonadav G. Shavit, Sebastien Krier, Mark Riedl

papers.title: Persistent Recursive Worlds Enable Autonomous Software Evolution
papers.summary: Software systems accumulate dependencies and design commitments over time, while the agents that modify them operate within bounded sessions. How, then, can development remain cumulative across generations of transient agents? We introduce EvoX Genesis, which organizes development as a persistent recursive software world. Agents enter an accepted repository version, delegate work within local scopes, and submit changes for verification and parent review. Once accepted, those changes pass to later episodes together with the contracts and tests used to assess them. The project thus preserves both earlier work and a basis for evaluating what comes next. We examine this continuity through four studies of formation, continuation and redevelopment. Starting without compiler code, Genesis built a C compiler with 219,676 lines of Rust source through 1,019 agent episodes over 123.4 hours. Within this growing implementation, repairs increased passes on a fixed set of 100 Csmith programs from 61 to 93; a subsequent revision retained all 93 passes. Development also continued in a separate compiler lineage when DeepSeek V4 Flash inherited a GLM 5.2 snapshot. To examine continuity when the implementation itself changes, Genesis redeveloped selected MESA functionality in Rust, with numerical agreement assessed against the Fortran reference across six workloads. The WebGL trajectory, meanwhile, exposed both repairs and regressions as repeated checks recorded progress towards 2,017/2,019 conformance pages passed. A complementary EvoX Compiler case connects program-merging performance to executable graph and backend contracts. Together, these records trace how accepted work becomes a foundation for further development: later agents inherit both usable implementations and concrete ways to assess further revisions.

authors.name: Beichen Huang, Zhenyu Liang, Bowen Zheng, Ran Cheng

papers.title: Semantic Prism: Generative Segmentation with an Explicit Semantic-Image Interface
papers.summary: Conditional image generators can render segmentation maps as semantic RGB images, but color drift and boundary mixing can undermine direct decoding. We present Semantic Prism, a framework that combines an explicit semantic-image interface with hierarchical refinement for road-scene segmentation. A generator adapted from a diffusion-distilled backbone produces a semantic RGB image with a single denoising update per crop. Distances to a fixed class-color codebook define interface logits and pixelwise class probabilities. Hierarchical Generator Evidence Alignment (HGEA) combines spatially aligned multilevel features from the VAE encoder of the generator with the input image, generated semantic image, and interface probabilities to predict additive corrections to these logits. Contextual Interface Hierarchy Disagreement (C-IHD) combines pointwise uncertainty, local context, and interface-refinement disagreement in a fixed score for ranking pixel errors, without an auxiliary predictor or an additional network pass. On the 500-image Cityscapes validation set, Semantic Prism achieves 72.07% mean mIoU, improving on direct-interface decoding by 11.39 percentage points. Extensive capacity-matched ablations show higher mean mIoU for multilevel refinement than for flat and single-level alternatives. The Cityscapes-trained model transfers to ACDC Dataset, achieving 46.89% mIoU without target-domain adaptation. Beyond Cityscapes, on BDD100K dataset, a separately trained model achieves 62.22% mIoU on its full 1,000-image validation set. Across the 3 evaluated datasets, C-IHD improves pixel-error area under the AUPR over uncertainty derived from maximum softmax probability, with segmentation predictions held fixed for each comparison. In particular, on ACDC, AUPR increases from 0.6580 to 0.7557, demonstrating that Semantic Prism presents more effective error ranking under adverse-condition domain shift.

authors.name: Weize Cai, Yongqi Dong, Zhida Shao, Zixin Fu, Xiaoxi Hu

papers.title: One Frozen Simulator Is Not Enough: Simulator Collapse in Multi-Agent RL
papers.summary: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) for human-AI interaction usually trains the agent against a single large language model (LLM) that simulates the user. We show that agents trained this way can systematically fail to generalize, and we trace the failure to simulator collapse: the simulator LLM is mode-collapsed, and a policy trained against it learns narrow strategies that exploit the simulator's mode behavior; these strategies transfer poorly to unseen simulators and to real users. We formalize the collapse and propose two solutions. Verbalized Sampling, applied at inference time, samples each simulator reply from a verbalized response distribution. Co-Training, applied during training similar to self-play, co-evolves the simulator as the policy, so the policy cannot exploit the mode behavior. A population variant samples the simulator for each rollout from a pool of recent checkpoints. We validate both solutions on three benchmarks: Persuasion for Good, tau^2-bench, and CooperBench. Verbalized Sampling improves held-out success by up to 9% over single-simulator RL, and Co-Training pushes gains further to 14%; the human study shows similar gain on real users. Both solutions also preserve the policy diversity that collapses under single-simulator RL. Overall, our findings on simulator collapse point to diverse simulators as a requirement for RL agents that serve real users. We release SCOPE, an open-source framework for Population Co-Training in multi-agent RL.

authors.name: Simon Yu, Nicholas Tomlin, Marwa Abdulhai, Ximing Lu, Derek Chong, Abe Hou, Dilara Soylu, Sergey Levine, Christopher D. Manning, Weiyan Shi

papers.title: Query Timing Produces Opposite Positional Biases Between LLMs and Humans
papers.summary: Positional biases such as recency and primacy effects have been documented in large language models (LLMs), yet the underlying mechanism by which these models make their evaluations remains poorly understood. Both primacy and recency biases have been observed in human judgments in response to evidence, but recent work suggest that when the listener updates their beliefs - during the presentation of evidence or only at the end - influences the presence of such effects. We investigate whether a similar phenomenon holds for LLMs, finding divergence from human behavior. These biases are more pronounced in newer models compared to their predecessors.

authors.name: Jasin Cekinmez, Addison J. Wu, Thomas L. Griffiths

papers.title: Sampling Luck Masquerades as Allocation Gain: Auditing Test-Time Budget Allocation for Neural Combinatorial Optimization
papers.summary: Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) solvers report the best of many sampled solutions per instance, and the sample count is, by convention, identical for every instance. Whether a non-uniform allocation of a fixed total budget would buy anything has not been measured. We measure it, and we audit the measurement itself. First, on in-distribution workloads the allocation headroom is not detectable. Across three pretrained solvers (POMO, AM, SymNCO) on uniform TSP-100, an oracle allocation computed and evaluated on the same stored samples reports a 2.2-2.6% gain with intervals excluding zero; measured out of sample the same gain is indistinguishable from zero (0.457, 0.015, -0.512 percent). Following the customary in-sample procedure, all three solvers would have supported a published 2%-level gain that does not exist. We calibrate this bias against an instance-wise null in which the true gain is zero by construction; over the ranges we test it does not shrink with more samples or more instances. Second, the same correction that removes the phantom gains preserves a real one. Under distribution shift (a workload mixing uniform and clustered instances), a pre-registered confirmatory experiment finds that allocation guided by held-out sample statistics improves best-of-k by 11.5% (AM, primary endpoint; 95% CI [7.4, 19.7]) and 12.0% (SymNCO, replication) at equal evaluation budget, with the signal-acquisition cost not charged; a pre-registered negative control (POMO, an order of magnitude more robust to shift) shows -0.3% [-0.7, 0.24]. The gain exceeds a frozen distribution-label baseline by 4.2 points [1.9, 7.7]. An exploratory policy charging a 20-sample probe against the same budget retains 3.4% (AM) and 4.6% (SymNCO). We give a correction procedure and a reporting checklist, and release all data, code, and the pre-registration record.

authors.name: Jinhyung Bae

papers.title: Why ML-based cough models do not generalize: a systematic cross-dataset evaluation for tuberculosis screening
papers.summary: Cough acoustics are promising for non-invasive tuberculosis (TB) screening, yet whether machine learning (ML) models capture disease-related acoustics or artifacts of data collection remains unresolved. We evaluated the cross-dataset generalizability of classical ML and deep learning (DL) cough-based TB classifiers across three independent datasets. Despite moderate within-dataset performance (ROC-AUC up to $0.76 \pm 0.06$), both pipelines fail to generalize, with external performance frequently below 0.6, indicating a possible limitation of the data. We further observed that audio representations are organized by recording device and dataset rather than TB status, predicted TB probability tracks country-level prevalence in CODA, and device mismatch degrades transfer while device-diverse training improves it. Additionally, a clinical-variable baseline generalizes more consistently (ROC-AUC $0.65-0.71$), indicating acquisition-specific variability in acoustics is a stronger driver of poor generalizability. High within-dataset performance is not enough. External validation is essential before cough-based TB models are clinically ready.

authors.name: Wensi Zhang, Tomas Teijeiro, J\'er\^ome Thevenot, David Atienza

papers.title: Learning Complementary Routes for Scouting Persimmon Orchards during Shoot Growth with CoverShare
papers.summary: At the study orchard, scouting during persimmon shoot growth focuses on leaf color change, leaf area, and internode length. Several routes may share an access lane, yet each can offer a view of row segments that the others miss. We introduce CoverShare to learn complementary routes under a fixed action budget. Within Policy Gradient for Parallel State Entropy maximization (PGPSE), CoverShare redistributes auxiliary rewards according to the state coverage lost when each policy is omitted and the number of policies visiting each state. It preserves the pooled entropy objective and total auxiliary reward. We simulated the annotated road network of a 6.7-ha site with 107 observable persimmon scouting units across five zones. At 40 actions per route, six distinct policies covered an expected 17.84 units perinspection, compared with 8.28 for six independent runs of one policy, averaged across eight training seeds. With the same policies trained on 40-action routes, extending each inspection route to 80 and 120 actions raised coverage to 22.52 and 28.38 units. Across seven public discrete-state tasks, CoverShare increased state support by a mean of 16.29% over the team-entropy baseline. Controlled ablations identified leave-one-policy-out coverage as the main contributor to these gains.

authors.name: Junhao Cao, Tao Wang, Zipeng Xie, Hongyi Xia, Jianian Wu, Lixia Huang

papers.title: Towards Efficient Auto-Interpretability of Boltz-1 Sparse Autoencoders
papers.summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) could turn AI models in Biology and other fields into engines of scientific discovery by explaining the superhuman capabilities of those models. We postulate that a latent is useful if we know three things: whether it is coherent, whether it can be described, and whether that description has predictive power. These questions are routinely conflated. We assemble them into a single pipeline and report some practical innovations. First, cross-seed dictionary stability prioritises which latents are worth spending resources to investigate. Second, an intruder-detection task asks whether a latent's activating examples share a recognizable pattern. Third, a separate pass proposes a candidate biological description which we convert into falsifiable predictions which can be tested in silico. Deployed on the Boltz-1 Pairformer trunk, stability prioritisation finds interpretable latents using about 4.4 times fewer latent evaluations each, and at 5.2 times lower measured LLM cost, while recovering over half of them. However, we notice that in our setup the LLM judge is heavily biased towards consistent residue identity and a simple filter that selects for features with high amino-acid identity precision outperforms the stability thresholding. This simpler method has the added benefit of requiring no extra SAE seeds but it remains uncertain if it reflects a genuinely useful heuristic or an limitation of the LLM judge.

authors.name: Piotr Jedryszek, Oliver M. Crook

papers.title: Representation Learning with Quantum Signal Processing
papers.summary: Representation learning begins when training changes the features that define similarity between data. A frozen-kernel model only reweights a fixed geometry. We establish quantum signal processing (QSP) as a solvable quantum model of the representation-learning regime. At arbitrary depth, we compute the exact mean and variance of its quantum neural tangent kernel, revealing an input-dependent angular geometry whose diagonal remains non-self-averaging even when the underlying unitary approaches Haar randomness. We also prove a sparse-data guarantee for the full nonlinear gradient flow without freezing or ensemble-averaging the kernel: the realized dynamics converges to an integrable scalar flow with a time-dependent kernel closure and explicit convergence times. A finite-depth speed limit holds for every data set and trajectory. At higher data density, numerical results show coupled evolution beyond both the scalar and frozen-kernel descriptions. These results give a controlled theory of learned quantum data geometry with provable training dynamics beyond the frozen limit.

authors.name: Junqi Wang, Junyu Liu

papers.title: Arabic Safety Alignment as Selective Refusal: An Empirical Study of SFT, DPO, and Guard Calibration
papers.summary: Arabic large language models must refuse harmful prompts without over-refusing benign or sensitive prompts, yet a single refusal rate hides this trade-off. We evaluate it using benign refusal B and harmful-prompt refusal H, where H measures refusal rather than harmful compliance. Across five Arabic-capable models and 130 runs on the full human-written AraSafe set, refusal-only supervised fine-tuning (SFT) collapses toward blanket refusal, whereas selected mixed-SFT configurations reach H = 90% to 93% at B = 14% to 23%; four selected configurations exceed the H = 90% target in all three runs, while Fanar does so in two of three. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and inference guards change B and H differently across models rather than acting as uniform upgrades. In a blinded 300-response audit, annotator binary-refusal agreement is 89.0% (kappa = 0.78); Qwen3Guard and Aya Expanse 32B reach 88.7% and 91.0% accuracy, respectively, with no conclusive paired difference. Selected SFT raises H on Arabizi for all five models, but none reaches 90%, showing only partial transfer from Modern Standard Arabic. Overall, the results support model-specific operating-point selection: set a deployment target and retain only interventions that improve it.

authors.name: Mohamad Zbib, Mohamad Bazzi, Ammar Mohanna

papers.title: The Safeguard Worked. Is the LLM System Safer?
papers.summary: Safeguards for large language model services are typically evaluated by their attack-blocking rates on test suites. Deployment decisions also depend on how much harmful assistance attackers can still obtain from the system, which these rates do not measure. To determine what published evaluations establish about deployment safety, we develop a framework that translates reported results into the minimum and maximum harmful assistance that can remain under a specified outcome and threat model. For safeguards that block attacks through a check, we show that the most an attacker can obtain depends on three properties: whether attack paths pass through the check, its miss rate against every attacker in the threat model, and how much assistance remains after a block. We apply this framework to 85 safeguard evaluations from 52 papers. Of these, only five argue that every attack path passes through the check, and four provide evidence on what remains after a block. These evidence gaps have practical consequences: in NeMo Guardrails' default streaming configuration, the check blocked 94% of password leaks in our test, yet the client received the password in every leak, blocked or not. We identify which of the three properties each safeguard category's evaluations omit, and what to measure for each of four ways attacks bypass a check. Deployments that require these measurements before launch can choose and configure safeguards that limit what attackers obtain from the deployed system.

authors.name: Pingyu Wu, Weiming Zhang, Nenghai Yu

papers.title: Amortizing Scaling Law Construction Costs
papers.summary: Scaling laws guide the design choices for training large foundation models, but deriving them involves training an exhaustive grid over hyperparameters, token budgets, and parameter counts, which is computationally expensive. Fitting a scaling law, however, only requires the best-loss frontier across compute scales, discarding most of the trained configurations. We propose a framework for efficient scaling law construction that formulates data collection as a Bayesian optimization problem, and introduce metrics for comparing scaling law fitting methods under constrained compute budgets. We find that progressively expanding the compute budget during acquisition, mirroring the compute-ordered evaluation of configurations in practice, substantially improves recovery efficiency. Augmenting the observed configurations with surrogate-fantasized evaluations then recovers the broader experimental grid, allowing accurate scaling law fitting without training every configuration. Together, these can closely match scaling law fits over a full dense grid at computational savings of up to $10\text{--}100\times$.

authors.name: Abhash Kumar Jha, Diana Alexandra Onu\c{t}u, Neeratyoy Mallik, Swagatam Haldar, Sam Laing, Niccol\`o Ajroldi, Shiwei Liu, Joaquin Vanschoren, Aaron Klein

papers.title: Structure Across Voices: Comparing acoustic-event type accumulation and sequence dependence across four vocal corpora using frozen audio encoders
papers.summary: Comparing acoustic structure across very different vocal corpora is difficult because the recordings use different native event units, contain different amounts of sequence, and were collected under different conditions. We use the high-dimensional representations of frozen, pretrained audio encoders to measure acoustic diversity and temporal organization. Matched sampling gives each corpus the same opportunities to observe new acoustic forms and relationships between events, without changing its native event definition. We compare sperm-whale codas, human speech phones, Bengalese-finch syllables, and common-marmoset calls using 1,952 events and 1,700 adjacent pairs per comparison. Whale shows the fastest accumulation of encoder-defined acoustic groups, while Finch has the strongest repeated-sequence recurrence against ordinary within-block shuffles. Their neighboring-event dependence is closely matched under a source-and-position control. A second preceding event changes held-out prediction more favorably for Whale than for the other corpora, although Whale's standalone improvement remains uncertain. Waveform measurements recover several differences, but duration and acquisition-sensitive properties also contribute. Together, the findings show how pretrained representations can measure distinct forms of vocal organization, while waveform and source controls define the scope of the comparison.

authors.name: Mudit Sinha, Sanika Chavan

papers.title: Uncovering Faithfulness Gaps in VLMs via Explanation-Driven Counterfactual Testing
papers.summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can produce Natural Language Explanations (NLEs) that sound plausible yet remain inconsistent with the visual evidence they cite. We present Explanation-Driven Counterfactual Testing (EDCT), an intervention-based protocol that extracts visual concepts cited in a model's explanation, applies verified minimal edits to them, and tests whether the resulting answer and explanation remain consistent with the edited image. Using this protocol, we create EDCT-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark spanning three complementary domains: knowledge-intensive visual question answering (OK-VQA), safety-critical driving (DriveLM), and 3D spatial reasoning (3DSRBench). Across the evaluated VLMs, EDCT reveals substantial faithfulness gaps, with models frequently producing responses inconsistent with verified visual changes. Finally, our fine-tuning study suggests that EDCT-generated counterfactuals provide high-impact training signals.

authors.name: Sihao Ding, Santosh Vasa, Aditi Ramadwar, Thomas Monninger

papers.title: RPMem: Learning Long-Term Recurrent Parametric Memory Across Sessions for LLM Agents
papers.summary: Long-running LLM agents require memory that persists and evolves across sessions. Text-based memory retrieves and reconstructs past interactions at every query, making long-horizon performance increasingly dependent on retrieval quality and contextual reasoning as histories grow. Parametric memory encodes experience directly into model computation, but existing approaches provide limited support for cross-session memory evolution. Their coupling to a specific backbone further restricts memory reuse after model replacement. We introduce RPMem, a two-stage architecture that compiles each session into a model-independent latent memory through forward computation and selectively integrates it with retained memory via a task-trained recurrent gate. The consolidated memory is then mapped to backbone-specific low-rank adaptation (LoRA) parameters, allowing the encoding capability to transfer when the backbone is replaced. Evaluation across three long-term memory benchmarks and five diverse backbones demonstrates broad generalization with near-constant update cost and memory footprint. With Qwen3-8B on PERMA, RPMem reaches 85.52%, outperforming the strongest parametric and text-based baselines by 5.32 and 12.98 percentage points, respectively. Ablations validate the complementary roles of session compilation and cross-session consolidation, while dynamics analyses reveal that the gate acquires task-specific memory integration strategies. These results establish RPMem as a lifecycle-independent parametric memory framework that maintains evolving cross-session memory that remains reusable across backbone replacements. Our code is available at https://github.com/Quark-Medical/rpmem/tree/main.

authors.name: Fanyu Zhao, Ruike Cao, Liang Dong, Fugen Yao, Jian Xu, Guanjun Jiang, Yifei Zhao, Yinsheng Li, Han Zhang

papers.title: FLARE: A Full-Lifecycle Dense Supervision Paradigm for Long-Horizon Coding Agents via Generative Reward Model
papers.summary: While test-time scaling enhances Large Language Model (LLM) agents in long-horizon software engineering (SWE), sparse binary rewards (Pass/Fail) create a severe credit assignment crisis and waste failed exploratory trajectories. Current trajectory optimization and scaling methods are costly and structurally limited, relying on heuristic state reuse without causal diagnosis or delayed scalar scoring without actionable online guidance. We propose FLARE (Full-Lifecycle Alignment and Reward Engine), a novel dense supervision paradigm driven by a lightweight Generative Reward Model (GRM). First, RADAR, an offline causal-aware diagnostic framework, extracts high-fidelity, hindsight-free supervision through causal-chain backtracking to distill a GRM providing real-time, step-level risk feedback. Second, FLARE uses this GRM to continuously optimize the agent across its entire lifecycle. During inference, FLARE acts as an Active Scaffold, autonomously intercepting high-risk generation steps for localized breakpoint re-execution, drastically reducing compute overhead. During post-training, the GRM's structured signals serve as process-supervised reranking scores for Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and step-level dense rewards for Reinforcement Learning (RL), mitigating policy collapse in sparse environments. Extensive evaluations show that FLARE establishes a new Pareto frontier across the agent lifecycle: FLARE (N=1) outperforms Global Rollout (N=5) with a 5x reduction in token consumption. Extending FLARE to training overcomes the sparse reward problem in long-horizon interactive tasks, delivering relative performance gains of 19.13% in SFT through process-aware data curation and a consistent 9.19% improvement in RL.

authors.name: Jingxuan Xu, Gang Wu, Yanan Wu, Yutao Mou, Songwei Yu, Tianzhuang He, Zhengshuo Gong, Zhao Liu, Zihang Xu, Wenqiang Zhu, Xinping Lei, Weihao Li, Ziqi Miao, Yuhui Bai, Zhongqiu Wang, Yan Wu, Ariel Deng

papers.title: Video-HopChain: Multi-Hop Questions and Confidence-Gated Exploration for Video Reasoning Models
papers.summary: HopChain has shown on still images that multi-hop data synthesis improves vision-language reasoning, because long chain-of-thought reasoning exposes errors that compound across steps, while most data used for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) rarely demands a chain of visual evidence, so these weaknesses are likely to stay unexposed. We observe the same problem in video, where this framework has not yet been explored. We therefore build Video-HopChain, a dataset of 22,550 multi-hop video questions over 13,378 videos, together with a held-out benchmark of 1,000 questions. Each question chains three to six yes/no questions about moments in one video, and each yields one of two integers depending on its answer. The final answer is the sum of these integers, so an exact match on that sum gives the verifiable reward that RLVR needs. We first train Qwen3-VL-8B with GRPO on a standard video dataset, and a second stage on Video-HopChain then raises the mean over eight video understanding and reasoning benchmarks from 55.4 to 57.9 and improves every one of them. Training on such a dataset, however, exposes a known limitation of GRPO: its learning signal comes from the reward variance within a group, so hard questions whose rollouts are all incorrect and easy questions whose rollouts are all correct both leave the group with no gradient. To recover these groups at the same compute budget, we introduce Confidence-Gated Exploration (CGE). With 8 rollouts per question, CGE samples the first 4 as usual. If these 4 are either all correct or all incorrect, it samples the last 4 with the policy's most confident token masked inside the reasoning span, and removes the masked positions from the loss while all 8 rollouts enter the advantage. With CGE, the mean rises further to 59.3. We release the dataset, the checkpoint, and the data generation and training code.

authors.name: Trung Nguyen Quang, Yuhao Dong, Shuo Sun, Shuai Liu, Shulin Tian, Kim-Hui Yap, Ziwei Liu

papers.title: Intuition Vectors from Pretrained Representations Steer Diffusion-Based Reasoning
papers.summary: Abstract visual reasoning requires identifying relationships between few examples and applying them to novel inputs. Recent advances have been driven by large language and vision-language models or specialized domain-specific architectures. It remains unclear whether abstract reasoning can be supported directly by the relational geometry of pretrained visual representations, without relying on language-based inference or task-specific representation learning. We investigate this possibility using frozen self-supervised vision encoders. With latent vector arithmetic, we confirmed that the representational geometry of two self-supervised encoders support abstract concept discrimination on Bongard problems and encode systematic relationships between input-output pairs in ARC tasks. Simple vector differences between image embeddings, which we call intuition vectors, capture transformations that generalize across instances of the same task. These vectors distinguish among 794 abstract reasoning tasks with up to 87.2\% accuracy, preserve relational structure across task-invariant visual transformations, and guide output retrieval for unseen inputs. Given this, we tested the hypothesis that this relational structure can steer generative reasoning by conditioning a diffusion transformer operating in pretrained visual latent space. On held-out ARC tasks, intuition-vector conditioning outperforms conditioning on complete demonstrations while requiring nearly six times less test-time compute, and supports zero-shot inference. Taken together, our findings suggest that pretrained visual representations provide a transferable substrate for abstract reasoning, enabling a modular approach in which the relational structure inferred from demonstrations steer generative reasoning.

authors.name: Shahar Haim, Daniel C. McNamee

papers.title: SkillPE: Creativity-Oriented Cinematic Skill Evolution for Text-to-Video Prompt Enhancement
papers.summary: Achieving high-quality cinematic text-to-video generation remains challenging for non-experts, whose prompts often lack professional narrative and creative design. Existing prompt enhancement (PE) methods and static cinematic skills offer limited capabilities for exploring diverse creative realizations. We propose SkillPE, a creativity-oriented PE framework that systematically evolves reusable cinematic skills through reference-guided exploration. Starting from expert-provided cinematic knowledge, SkillPE initializes and normalizes 20 structured seed skills. It then retrieves movie references categorized as resonators (good matches), dissonants (weak matches), and divergents (creatively inspiring near-misses). Resonators and dissonants refine skill applicability and execution, while divergents inspire alternative cinematic realizations through controlled mutations that preserve user intent. Candidate skills are assessed through generated videos along prompt fidelity, cinematic quality, narrative appeal, and creativity to construct the final skill libraries. Experiments on StoryEval and VBench demonstrate improvements of up to 1.10 points over seed skills and 1.02 points over the strongest external baseline on a 7-point four-dimensional evaluation scale. Overall, SkillPE offers a practical approach to balancing fidelity and creativity in cinematic text-to-video generation.

authors.name: Yanwei Huang, Mingxuan Zhu, Shujie Li, Shiyuan Liu, Yuanxing Zhang, Arpit Narechania

papers.title: Representable but Unlearned: Encoding Rank and the Interaction-Prediction Floor
papers.summary: Input encodings can prevent a predictor from reproducing measured interactions jointly, even when each interaction is individually representable. We compute the attainable contrast space from the encoder and contrast design, without labels or predictor fitting. Projecting measured contrasts onto this space gives an empirical squared-error floor for any deterministic decoder using the encoding. On an siRNA panel, a graph neural network's training-only feature mask merges 165 measured states into 90 classes, reducing the rank of 140 interaction contrasts to 72. The floor is 0.009980, or 14.63% of recorded contrast energy, the mean squared error of predicting zero for every contrast. Its 14.6% share of fitted interaction error adds little: predicted interactions are nearly zero, and their MSE of 0.068335 slightly exceeds that of the same control. Antisense-marginal shares are larger: 36.49% of recorded energy and 38.1% of fitted error. Three restored chemistry columns suffice for full rank. Removing the full mask eliminates the floor, but refitting improves interaction MSE by only 0.000017; the restored features remain absent from training inputs. Two further panels clarify the diagnostic's scope. A released splicing predictor encodes injectively and retains the full design rank of 1,986, so its floor is zero. For an independent count-fingerprint encoder on a lipid panel, 800 pairwise-distinct encoded contrast rows have rank 740, exposing 60 restrictions missed by duplicate-row checks. The diagnostic identifies encoding-imposed limits and can trace them to specific features. It separates representability from learned accuracy, but does not by itself predict refitting gains or explain the remaining error.

authors.name: Zahra Khodagholi, Niloofar Yousefi

papers.title: LeapQuant: Efficient Linear Attention with Accurate Recurrent State Quantization
papers.summary: Recent LLMs increasingly adopt hybrid designs that replace standard attention with linear attention, such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN) and Kimi Delta Attention (KDA). Although they compress the context into a fixed-size recurrent state and substantially reduce the cost of long-context processing, repeatedly reading and updating that state remains a major inference bottleneck. Quantization offers a natural way to reduce this cost, but can significantly degrade model quality, due to the accumulation of rounding errors and the presence of outlier rows and columns in the state. To address these challenges, we propose LeapQuant, a training-free method that achieves near-lossless performance under 8-bit recurrent-state quantization. First, to mitigate error accumulation, we propose per-window quantization, which leaps over a window of tokens and quantizes the state only once at its end. Within a window, outputs are computed from the fixed low-bit state together with high-precision buffered updates. Second, to reduce the error introduced by each quantization, LeapQuant retains the state's largest outliers as a few high-precision Compensator Tokens, which share the update path of real tokens. We then smooth the remaining residual before quantization to further reduce the error. Comprehensive experiments across the Qwen, Kimi, and GLM model families show that LeapQuant substantially reduces memory and compute costs during inference. With accuracy comparable to the FP32 baseline, it achieves average speedups of 2.05--3.70$\times$ at the kernel level and 1.47$\times$ for end-to-end inference on NVIDIA B200, RTX PRO 6000, and RTX 5090 GPUs.

authors.name: Yi Pan, Haocheng Xi, Kan Zhu, Xingyang Li, Yibo Wu, Mayank Mishra, Hongtao Zhang, William X. Zheng, Baris Kasikci, Song Han, Kurt Keutzer, Rishabh Iyer, Ion Stoica

papers.title: Pseudo-Label-Triggered Retraining from Forecast Errors for Online Time Series Forecasting
papers.summary: Real-world time series forecasting systems operate under non-stationary data streams, where forecasting performance may degrade over time. Although retraining can recover the performance, it incurs non-trivial computational and operational costs. Under limited deployment resources, the key challenge is therefore not only how to retrain but also when to retrain. While existing retraining policies often rely on indirect indicators such as drift alarms or model staleness, we instead use realized forecast errors as direct deployment feedback. In this paper, we propose PILOT (Pseudo-label-Informed Learned Online Trigger), an online retraining framework that learns when to retrain from forecast-error dynamics. Since ground-truth retraining labels are unavailable, PILOT constructs a pseudo-label from future increases in forecast error and trains a lightweight scorer to predict it from observed error states. At deployment, PILOT uses only completed forecast errors and serves as a plug-in module for arbitrary forecasting backbones without architectural modification. We evaluate PILOT under standard multivariate forecasting settings across eight benchmarks with three representative backbones---DLinear, iTransformer, and TimesNet. Across all three backbones, PILOT achieves state-of-the-art average-rank performance among retraining policies while maintaining a favorable performance--efficiency trade-off.

authors.name: Yeryeong Kwak, Yoo-Min Jung, Jonghun Park

papers.title: Misalignment of Low-Loss Regions Causes Grokking
papers.summary: Grokking refers to the delayed emergence of validation-set generalization after a model has already overfit the training set. Although first observed in small algorithmic tasks trained with transformers, its underlying mechanism remains unsettled. In this work, we develop an analysis framework based on mode connectivity and the geometry of low-loss regions. The framework predicts that the standard modular-arithmetic setting does not always produce grokking: under a symmetry-preserving train/validation split, we observe a stable anti-grokking case in which validation performance does not recover. This counterexample challenges several existing correlational explanations of grokking. More broadly, our analysis framework and results further suggest that grokking arises when the low-loss regions induced by the training and validation partitions are misaligned. Once these regions become well aligned, training hyperparameters alone cannot produce grokking and the observed dynamics collapse to either trainable or non-trainable behavior.

authors.name: Yongding Tian, Zaid Al-Ars, Maksim Kitsak, Peter Hofstee

papers.title: AEGIS: Differentiable Mars Climate Model with Neural Closures
papers.summary: General circulation models (GCMs) are the primary tool for simulating planetary atmospheres. They play a vital role in understanding Mars's atmosphere, as forecasting its unique weather is mission-critical for operations such as entry, descent, and landing. Mars poses unusual challenges for these models, as observations are sparse compared to Earth. In addition, a thin $CO_2$ atmosphere alongside a radiatively active dust cycle creates a volatile atmosphere with large diurnal temperature swings and no true terrestrial analog for validation. Existing Mars GCMs, including the LMD PCM, the NASA Ames Mars GCM, and PlanetWRF, are mature and physically detailed but are implemented in legacy Fortran with finite-difference or finite-volume solvers, and they do not expose gradients for calibration or machine learning. Here we present AEGIS, a modular differentiable Mars climate model that couples Mars's unique atmospheric physics to the Dinosaur dynamical core, with interfaces for neural closures. We showcase stable ten-Mars-year simulations that reproduce the seasonal $CO_2$ cycle while conserving the total $CO_2$ inventory, capture realistic large-scale surface-temperature structure, and produce surface pressure that follows Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) topography. Gradients through coupled trajectories agree with finite differences and support physical calibration and neural training. We compare with conventional GCMs, highlighting the framework's computational efficiency and differentiability.

authors.name: Sameera S Kashyap, Victor Cruz, Angel Yepez, Razvan Marinescu

papers.title: Can Power Draw Constrain Covert Compute? Limits of Analogue Verification for AI Governance
papers.summary: Frontier AI treaties or agreements on limiting computation require external verification; an external auditor must be able to confirm how much computation actually ran and that parties are adhering to the agreement. Analogue, off-chip measurements such as power draw provide an information channel for verification. It is unknown how well these analogue channels can constrain the amount of computation against an adversary who actively tries to subvert the audit. We derive a closed form for $\beta$, the largest hidden computation a power trace cannot exclude, as a fraction of the declared machine capacity. Measurements on NVIDIA A100 GPUs give $\beta = 1.16$ in the worst case, while an adversarial matched-energy schedule hides at least $0.41$. Analogue power measurements alone therefore constrain compute weakly. Additional restrictions granted by the threat model, such as the ability of the verifier to re-execute the declared work at an observed operating point, let the verifier push $\beta$ down to $0.059$ in the maximally restricted case. This gives a quantitative estimate of what analogue measurements can contribute to compute verification.

authors.name: Tom Kimpson, Mauricio Baker, Emlyn Graham

papers.title: Natural Code Transformation Confuses Agents in Vulnerability Analysis
papers.summary: Having demonstrated a strong potential for automating vulnerability discovery, AI agents can also be used to attack software systems at scale. Today's software systems need mechanisms to level the playing field by slowing down potential attacks, giving them time to patch vulnerabilities and strengthen software. Along this line, our study of agent trajectories in vulnerability analysis shows a surprising finding: agents produce dramatically different results across real-world code commits that carry the same functionality and the same vulnerability. This phenomenon appears consistently in multiple code domains and vulnerability categories. It motivates us to study natural and functionality-preserving code transformations derived from real-world software development, and their potential as a defense against attacker agents. We build a corpus of natural transformations by mining recurring development patterns from real-world code commits, and apply them to evaluate impact on agentic vulnerability analysis. Our results show that even a single form of transformation can effectively "confuse" frontier agents, e.g., Claude Mythos 5.2 with Claude Code, reducing successes in vulnerability discovery. We also study different agent failures, whether transformations can be composed to provide stronger protection, and adaptive attackers who seek to reverse them. Overall, our study of natural code transformation significantly expands the research space of using code transformations to defend against malicious agents.

authors.name: Jie Zhu, Ronik Bhaskar, Heather Zheng, Ben Y. Zhao, Kexin Pei

papers.title: SarcasTraps: Effect of Sarcasm on Turkish Hate Speech Detection
papers.summary: Standard hate speech detection datasets often emphasize explicit harmful language, but directed harm can also be expressed indirectly, without clearly hateful wording. Sarcasm is one such form of indirect expression, as it can convey harmful intent through mock praise, exaggeration, humor, or apparent politeness. In this paper, we introduce SarcasTraps, a targeted external test set for analyzing the effect of sarcasm on Turkish hate speech detection. SarcasTraps contains 479 entries annotated along two dimensions: hate speech and sarcasm. We train classifiers using BERTurk and XLM-RoBERTa on two existing Turkish hate speech datasets and evaluate them on SarcasTraps, using it strictly as an external test set. We also evaluate GPT-4.1 and Llama-3.3-70B in a zero-shot setting on SarcasTraps. Results show that sarcasm substantially affects hate speech detection. Fine-tuned encoder models lose recall on sarcastic hate, while zero-shot LLMs maintain higher recall but suffer substantial precision drops on sarcastic examples. These findings show that both fine-tuned hate speech detectors and zero-shot LLMs struggle when sarcasm is involved, and SarcasTraps provides quantitative evidence of this challenge through a targeted Turkish test set. Due to the presence of sensitive and hateful language, SarcasTraps will be shared upon request for academic research purposes. Warning: This paper has examples from the dataset which contains offensive and hateful content towards groups of people.

authors.name: Niyazi Ahmet Metin, Dilara Kek\"ull\"uo\u{g}lu

papers.title: Let the Mind Conceive, Let the Hand Achieve: Coupling Grounded Action and Progress Evaluation for Long-Horizon Manipulation
papers.summary: A robot following a multi-step instruction needs to act on the right objects in the right order, even as the scene changes. It must also maintain awareness of task progress and determine when to advance. To address these challenges, we introduce Orchestra, an agent harness that separates task planning and execution management from action generation. Orchestra decomposes a complete multimodal instruction into ordered subtasks, tracks completed steps, and updates the locations of relevant objects and destinations during execution. It maintains a shared context containing the active subtask, spatial grounding, and recent observations. An action policy uses this context to generate actions, while a separately trained progress evaluator estimates when to advance to the next subtask. To evaluate whether robots trained on atomic instructions and short trajectories can execute longer subtask sequences, we introduce a benchmark named RMBench-Compose. Orchestra achieves a mean success rate of $68.22\%$ across nine RMBench tasks, outperforming Mem-0 by $26.22$ percentage points. On RMBench-Compose, it achieves an Average Success Length (ASL) of $7.35$ subtasks, $2.46$ times that of HarnessVLA. Across four real-world multi-step tasks, it improves mean ASL by $25.0\%$ over Orchestra using the base $\pi_{0.5}$ policy. These results show that Orchestra helps robots carry out longer sequences of subtasks while preserving the requested subtask order and acting on the specified objects. Our code and project page are available at https://youpengwen.github.io/Orchestra

authors.name: Youpeng Wen, Gang Wang, Tianyu Huang, Weiwei Zhang, Zhijian Huang, Wei Chen, Xieyuanli Chen, Yunhui Liu

papers.title: Does On-Policy Distillation Need to Complete Every Rollout?
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher knowledge to a student through feedback on student-generated rollouts, but generating complete rollouts and computing per-token teacher feedback are computationally expensive. Existing truncation methods save computation by stopping rollouts early. However, they do not compensate for truncated token gradients, which biases the gradient estimates and changes Vanilla OPD's original training objective. Furthermore, their truncation decisions rely on assumptions about supervision quality or criteria that may not generalize across settings. We introduce Stochastic Truncated On-Policy Distillation (STOPD), which accelerates OPD by randomly truncating student rollouts and correcting the resulting sampling bias with blockwise inverse-probability weighting (IPW). At each training step, we sample a stopping position for each rollout before generation and let the student generate until that position or natural termination. We obtain teacher feedback on every generated token and use blockwise IPW to compensate for the lower probability of retaining later tokens while controlling the weights. We prove that this weighting preserves Vanilla OPD's gradient sum in expectation and derive one-step update-error bounds for SGD, Adam, and Muon. We evaluate STOPD across multiple teacher-student model pairs, task domains, and optimizers. STOPD reduces generated tokens by 25-48% while maintaining accuracy comparable to Vanilla OPD, achieving 1.3-2.2x training speedups.

authors.name: Zhengxin Zhang, Maosen Tang, Ning Wang, Changhao Li, Jingren Zhou, Bo Dai, Sainyam Galhotra, Alex Townsend, Claire Cardie

papers.title: Forecasting Retail Sales at Every Grain: Trees, Foundation Models, Transformers and World Models Compared on Four Public Data Sets
papers.summary: A retailer makes decisions from the same demand at different grains: store orders by item and day, promotions by item and week, category reviews and supplier terms. This paper asks whether one forecast, built at the finest grain and summed to every coarser grain, can serve them all, and which model does that best. It compares LightGBM, pretrained foundation models (TimesFM, Chronos-Bolt, Timestral), the Temporal Fusion Transformer and a world model that carries each item's state forward under the price and promotion plan, on M5, six Dominick's categories, Breakfast at the Frat and Corporacion Favorita, with the world model and LightGBM tuned by a common search. When to use the average: the average of the tuned world model and LightGBM, summed to every grain, has the lowest error in 22 of 27 grain and data set cases and is never the least accurate on the final held-out periods. When to use the world model: on existing items kept out of training it loses at most 0.040 in scaled error, against up to 0.311 for LightGBM, and on lines with short history it is clearly more accurate on six of nine data sets. When to use LightGBM: on heavily promoted lines, fast sellers and lines with long history (six of nine data sets each) and in price-cut weeks. Inconclusive: lines never promoted and slow lines are close to even, and 52 weeks ahead the average is the most accurate on five of seven data sets, with the world model ahead of LightGBM on two of seven. The findings hold for these data sets and the price and promotion levers; anyone adopting them should rerun every comparison on their own data.

authors.name: Karthik Iyer, Madan Dabbeeru

papers.title: Activation-Space Exploration for Visual and Textual Reasoning with RLVR
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves visual and textual reasoning by sampling responses, scoring them with an automatic verifier, and updating the policy from the resulting rewards. The policy therefore receives direct learning signals only from trajectories that appear in its rollouts. Yet repeated sampling from the same policy can concentrate on similar reasoning paths, leaving useful alternatives unexplored under a fixed rollout budget. We introduce Activation-Space Exploration (ASE), an online method for diversifying training rollouts. By clustering activation differences between correct and incorrect responses to the same problem, ASE builds a structured bank of latent exploration vectors. Different vectors are then applied to subsequent rollouts to explore alternative reasoning paths. Under the same rollout budget, ASE improves average accuracy over GRPO on Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct by 5.41 and 3.15 percentage points across six visual mathematical and six general visual reasoning benchmarks, respectively. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base, it improves average Mean@8 over GRPO across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks by 4.87 percentage points, with gains also observed on Qwen3-8B-Base.

authors.name: Yunan Zeng, Jinhao Jing, Xi Cheng, Yuwang Wang

papers.title: REGER: Modeling inter-item Relations with Semantic IDs for Generative Recommendation
papers.summary: Personalized recommendation depends on learning semantic and collaborative relations among items from online content and user interactions. Generative recommendation (GR) offers a promising paradigm by autoregressively generating discrete semantic IDs (SIDs) of items. However, randomly initialized SID token embeddings and GR models trained from scratch do not directly inherit the semantic relations inherent in items, while inter-item collaborative relations are learned largely implicitly through token-level attention and next-token supervision. To address this limitation, we propose REGER, a unified framework that explicitly incorporates inter-item relations into semantic pretraining, history encoding, and SID generation. We pretrain the GR model through generative semantic retrieval, enabling it to inherit inter-item semantic similarity by learning to generate semantic neighbors' SIDs. We combine global attention with local attention aligned with SID boundaries to capture historical context and directed transitions between adjacent items. We formalize item-level preference distillation on the SID prefix tree, deriving an exact factorization of item preference distributions into prefix conditionals and a weighted decomposition of item-level KL divergence into conditional KL terms. Guided by this decomposition, we renormalize the generator's probabilities over legal next tokens and match the resulting distributions to the teacher's conditional preferences along the ground-truth SID path, jointly optimizing the distillation objective with cross-entropy. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed preference distillation and demonstrate that REGER consistently outperforms existing GR baselines while retaining efficient inference.

authors.name: Yuxi Huang, Silin Zhou, Chenhao Wang, Zihan Li, Gangming Guo, Pei Ke, Lisi Chen, Shen Gao, Shuo Shang

papers.title: Cassette-Editor: Shared Timeline Semantics for Human and Agent Editing
papers.summary: Video editing involves tedious manual manipulation across interconnected timeline tracks, motivating automated agents that offload routine work while keeping the project directly revisable by humans. Fixed operation catalogs limit expressiveness, while even a basic trim requires coordinated updates across later clips, attached titles, and transitions. We present Cassette-Editor, an agent harness that unifies manual user gestures and automated agent patches within a shared editing environment. The shared action language expresses the editor's manual content changes, and a common history records committed edits for undo and manual refinement. When the model selects an edit, a state executor automatically derives its downstream consequences, such as shifting later clips and attached titles after a trim, while a validation rulebook enforces structural invariants and returns localized diagnostics for automated repair. To keep the agent grounded as the project evolves, dynamic read operations map transcripts and shot descriptions onto the current timeline. Evaluated with GPT-6 Luna, the full harness passed the scored request checks in 92/93 trials across 31 authored requests on two interview documentaries, compared with 48/93 for an internal basic-tools baseline. In ablations, disabling the consequences derived by the executor reduced passed trials from 230/232 to 199/232 on edits with dependent timeline elements, while ablating rulebook validation and repair lowered passed trials from 46/48 to 10/48 on requests operating near structural validity boundaries. Evaluating the complete system on 50 TVSum videos further demonstrated greater agreement with human annotations than a general agent using the same model (F1 23.8 vs. 20.1).

authors.name: Zhixin Zeng, Jiahao Zhong

papers.title: WorldFlow: Joint Video and 3D Motion Prediction via Large-Scale Pretraining
papers.summary: Predicting future physical states stands as a central challenge in embodied intelligence.
