However, the role of stochasticity in the diffusion model-sampler across denoising remains poorly understood. We introduce a per-timestep counterfactual diagnostic that tests how changing the sampled noise affects the final output. Across five model-sampler configurations spanning three robotics benchmarks, diverse architectures, domains, and conditioning mechanisms, we reveal highly varied temporal sensitivity profiles, where noise-induced deviations can amplify, partially contract, or undergo near-total attenuation downstream. From these profiles, we define stochastic diversity windows (SDWs): compact intervals that identify where sampler stochasticity has the strongest measured influence on the final output. Guided by these windows, we apply two heuristic interventions: targeted stochastic amplification, which increases sample diversity exploration of the solution space, and an SDW-hybrid sampler, which replaces DDPM steps with DDIM skips in low-impact regions, resulting in network evaluation reductions of up to 40-60% and wall-clock time by up to 85%, with no consistent changes detected in feasibility, cost, or diversity across held-out tasks.

authors.name: Tina Lakhani, Jing Wu, Yu-Kun Lai, Ze Ji

papers.title: Robust Actor-Critic Learning under Transport and Divergence Uncertainty
papers.summary: Learning reliable control policies requires accounting for uncertainty in transition dynamics and errors introduced by function estimation and action generation. We develop an actor--critic method for discounted robust Markov decision processes with continuous states and actions and an unknown nominal transition law. We consider transition uncertainty sets defined by Wasserstein distance, total variation, Kullback--Leibler divergence, or Pearson chi-square divergence. A conditional diffusion model is fitted once to offline transitions. At each subsequent iteration, we estimate the robust action-value function from current-policy observations using a shared-target minimax criterion, then update a generative actor through exponentially weighted score matching. Regularization preserves exploration and provides the density regularity needed for conditional distribution estimation. Under coverage and regularity conditions, we establish finite-sample bounds for critic estimation, the learned conditional action law, and the robust return of the implemented policy. The bounds distinguish critic estimation error, uncertainty in the nominal transition model, and policy regularization, and characterize how the four robustness radii affect the resulting guarantees.

authors.name: Kunqi Huang, Lican Kang, Hongrui Shu, Jincheng Ying

papers.title: TabDAG: Structured Evolutionary Search for Tabular Feature Engineering
papers.summary: Feature engineering can improve tabular prediction, but useful transformations are compositional, data-dependent, and subject to leakage constraints. We present TabDAG, a framework that combines evolutionary search with a graph representation of feature-engineering programs. Nodes implement row-wise or data-fitted transformations; edges encode dependencies among raw variables, intermediate values, and final features. The representation supports interactions, statistical encodings, clustering- and neighborhood-based features, and multi-stage compositions in a single executable program. Mutations are structured edits constrained by a parent-specific schema and checked before evaluation. In our experiments, no structurally invalid program reached evaluation, although proposals could be rejected and valid graphs could still fail at runtime. Across ten regression and classification datasets and three tabular model families, evolved features improve predictive performance over raw inputs. TabDAG and its combination with OpenFE achieve the two best mean ranks among the compared methods; pairwise rank differences between feature-engineering methods do not survive multiple-testing correction. The LLM-based searches use the same backbone and candidate-evaluation budget. A controlled ablation compares free-form Python, whole-graph JSON, and constrained graph edits with the search engine, budget, and backbone held fixed. Constrained edits yield fewer failed evaluations than either rewrite baseline. The resulting graphs expose the transformations and dependencies selected by search, enabling feature-level analysis of the observed gains.

authors.name: Anastasia Volkova (FusionBrain Lab), Andrey Kuznetsov (FusionBrain Lab), Ivan Oseledets (AXXX), Valentin Khrulkov (FusionBrain Lab, AXXX)

papers.title: Symmetries of Counterfactuals: Identification and Testability of Counterfactual Maps from Covariate Heterogeneity
papers.summary: In general, counterfactuals are not identified from data alone, because many causal models produce the same observed distributions but different counterfactuals. A common approach to circumvent this problem is to restrict the mechanism to a class in which it becomes unique, such as triangular monotone maps or optimal transport maps. However, whether the assumed class is correct is usually not examined. In this work, we study what the data can tell us when covariates are available that influence the outcome only through its latent cause. First, we characterise all counterfactual maps that are consistent with the data. They differ from the true map by a group of symmetries that preserve the conditional outcome distributions given the covariates. The more these distributions vary across covariate values, the smaller the group. Second, we show that for the classes above, consistency with the data is equivalent to a single conditional independence, which yields a test of the assumed class. We illustrate both results on synthetic data and on the ACTG 175 HIV trial.

authors.name: Marc Braun, Adel Daoud, Jose M. Pe\~na

papers.title: Is model self-assessment enough for diverse LVLM ensembles?
papers.summary: Ensembles of diverse Large Vision Language Models have demonstrated performance beyond that of single models across multiple datasets and tasks. However, the necessary aggregation process usually relies on training, parameter fitting, or complex task-specific pipelines. Furthermore, evaluation is limited, making a fair comparison difficult. We create a unified pipeline where we perform candidate response selection: we build an ensemble by selecting the best answer from a set provided by different models. We comprehensively evaluate across 34 different means of confidence estimation, 24 ensemble configurations, 20 datasets, and two prompt specifications. We show that simple training and parameter-free approaches can be sufficient, even for ensembles of different architectures. These simple self-assessment approaches rely solely on each constituent model's confidence, without explicit calibration, yet are able to perform better than said constituent models. They are also competitive with more involved alternatives on standard metrics such as accuracy, including on open-ended problems. However, we also discover that dataset, ensemble composition, and prompt wording are key confounding variables insufficiently explored by prior work that significantly affect ensemble performance, such that the ensemble can perform worse than its best constituent model. These must be optimized for to get the most out of ensembles, at the cost of limiting their generalizability. We recommend that practitioners consider training-free ensembles only if deployment conditions can be precisely characterized, with Best-of-N configurations of strong models being a good starting point.

authors.name: Michael Smith, Frank P. Ferrie

papers.title: When Anchors Shift the Target: Advantage-Gated Adaptation for Diffusion Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary: Forward-process reinforcement learning adapts diffusion and flow-matching models by re-noising rewarded generations into regression targets. Because negative advantages induce concave updates with unbounded repulsive gradients, existing methods stabilize training using cached predictions from a moving policy copy, yet these anchors also alter what positive feedback teaches the model to fit. We formalize this conflict as anchor coupling: after separating frozen-reference regularizers, affine moving-anchor rules cannot eliminate negative curvature while preserving every positive regression target. We propose Advantage-Gated Adaptation (AGA) to decouple these roles. Positive samples retain standard target fitting, whose self-limiting update vanishes at the observed target independently of the moving anchor. Negative samples instead use the first-order tangent of the concave objective at the moving-policy prediction, preserving the local repulsion direction with a prediction-independent gradient. Within the quadratic-anchor family, these requirements uniquely determine the parameter-free gate $\omega(a)=\max(-a,0)$. Because the moving copy provides local linearization rather than retention, AGA assigns long-horizon behavior preservation to a frozen pretrained reference regularized at its operating classifier-free guidance scale, interpreted through an implicit-reward lens. Across compositional generation, text rendering, and preference alignment, our experiments show that displacing positive targets degrades visual quality and heightens sensitivity to policy-copy schedules, whereas AGA consistently improves the reward--quality trade-off.

authors.name: Pu Cao, Min Zhou, Ying Shu, Tiezheng Ge, Qing Song, Lu Yang

papers.title: Uncovering the Invisible in Routine Radiology: Cross-Modal Detection of MRI-Verified Soft-Tissue Pathologies from CBCT via Physics-Guided 3D Self-Supervised Learning
papers.summary: Routine X-ray modalities like cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) are optimized for high-contrast mineralized tissues, leaving soft-tissue abnormalities buried beneath photon noise and below human visual perception. Thus, detecting non-calcified pathologies requires secondary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). We demonstrate that sub-visual radiographic signatures of soft-tissue pathology are physically preserved within routine CBCT scans and can be extracted for opportunistic screening using a targeted, physics-guided deep learning pipeline, even under extreme paired-data scarcity. Using the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) as a model system (N = 212 paired CBCT-MRI joints), we address the severe overfitting of high-capacity 3D networks through a two-stage framework. First, we employ a frozen full-grid 3D masked autoencoder (BertsWin) pre-trained on 6,550 unlabeled CBCT volumes via the GradientConductor (GCond) optimizer and an anatomy-aware objective (PhysLoss) redirecting gradient flow into the [-300, 300] HU soft-tissue window. Second, automated localization of the condylar zenith drives a deterministic 3D cropping that eliminates 81% of background osseous variance. Evaluated via a patient-isolated 3x10-fold stratified cross-validation protocol, a statistically robust sub-visual signal for MRI-verified synovial effusion (ROC AUC = 0.793) emerges exclusively from representations pre-trained with the PhysLoss and GCond regime. Crucially, only this setup captures true 3D anatomical chirality (p < 0.001) and high intra-patient structural consistency (0.791) over inter-patient noise; conversely, identical architectures pre-trained with standard L2 loss or unmasked variance decomposition (MVC) collapse to random guessing. These findings establish a generalizable paradigm for repurposing routine, low-contrast radiographic scans into opportunistic screening tools for occult soft-tissue disease.

authors.name: Evgeny Alves Limarenko

papers.title: Reversing the text is not reversing the path: a fixed-text measure without a zero, and an assembly-order comparison that vanishes identically
papers.summary: For an ensemble of trajectories the fluctuation theorems give the entropy production its meaning and zero. The same expression has recently been evaluated on one fixed text, $\Delta = [\log P(x) - \log P(\tilde x)]/L$ with $\tilde x$ the text in reversed order, read as an entropy production separating causally from arbitrarily ordered prose. A single text is neither a distribution nor a dynamics, and the texts at issue were produced by other models. No theorem fixes where the zero of a fixed-text quantity lies: the expression carries over from an ensemble, its zero does not. We supply a zero from an exact antisymmetry. Scoring a text's $n$ sentences in all $n!$ orders, reversal carries $\pi$ to $\pi \circ \mathrm{rev}$, a measure-preserving involution, so $\Delta(\pi) = -\Delta(\pi \circ \mathrm{rev})$ identically and the values are centred at zero for any score. The authored arrangement's midrank is then unitless, bounded, and 0.50 for a score blind to order. Across five autoregressive evaluators from 124M to 4B parameters, and taking the prompt-defined labels at face value, 8% to 15% of the median midrank's distance from the null is attributable to causal order and the rest to the arrangement being the order the passage was produced in. The thermodynamic reading needs a comparison whose zero does hold on the text read, and a masked model supplies one: the any-order chain rule gives a genuine log-probability, and its left-to-right and right-to-left orders for one text give $\sigma$, a comparison of two assembly orders. Both run from the empty sequence to the same text, so it is not a path against its time reverse. It vanishes identically when the evaluator's conditionals come from a joint, and a non-zero reading reports the evaluator's incompatibility, not the text. Neither is a fixed-text entropy production, for different reasons.

authors.name: Y. -H. Taguchi

papers.title: Magflow: Differentiable Simulation of Industrial-Grade 6D Magnetic Levitation
papers.summary: Magnetic levitation with six-degrees-of-freedom enables frictionless transport and micrometer-scale positioning in principle, but low-level control is inherently challenging due to its complex and unstable dynamics. Industrial systems typically rely on deep hardware-software co-design, where mover and stator geometries are jointly designed to enable a compact, hand-crafted approximation of the electromagnetic force computation, thereby keeping control computationally tractable at kilohertz rates. However, this approach imposes overly conservative constraints on the operating workspace and the range of supported mover topologies. Instead of reducing the underlying physics to a hand-crafted approximation, we compute the physics directly. We introduce Magflow, a fully differentiable, GPU-parallel simulator for 6D magnetic levitation. It is used to train the first neural controller for an industrial-grade 6D magnetic levitation system that is learned purely from simulated physics. We show that the learned neural controller transfers zero-shot from simulation to real hardware while satisfying hard real-time constraints at 4 kHz. The learned controller achieves qualitatively new behaviors and even levitates a mover topology for which no hand-crafted solution exists. These results demonstrate that co-design is not a physical necessity for 6D magnetic levitation control. More broadly, control learning from simulated physics can find solutions beyond the reach of control engineering in demanding industrial domains. Source code and demonstration videos are publicly available at https://sites.google.com/view/magflow.

authors.name: Philipp Hartmann, Jannick Strangh\"oner, Klaus Neumann

papers.title: Amortizing Tempered Sampling with Corrected Self-Training
papers.summary: Learning a neural sampler can reduce the cost of repeated sampling from an un-normalized distribution, but obtaining good training data remains difficult. We develop a corrected self-training scheme across a sequence of tempered targets, making use of importance sampling and Markov chain Monte Carlo to correct the samples and replay buffers to store them. We introduce Sequential Score Sampler (SSS) as a particular case. In SSS, the proposal is a score-based diffusion trained by regression on energy gradients; and the samples are corrected by importance weights on the path space. After training, samples can be collected directly from the model, from its importance-corrected proposals, or from the final-temperature buffer. The method amortizes repeated sampling by encoding the global structure of the target in the model. SSS achieves competitive sampling accuracy across the benchmarks and, on several targets, uses shorter runtimes with fewer energy evaluations than competing samplers.

authors.name: Hoang-Viet Nguyen, Hai-Dang Dau, Alexandre H. Thi\'ery

papers.title: Event-Based Dynamic Lip Region Estimation During Speech
papers.summary: Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and low power consumption, making them promising for speech-related applications. These include automatic lip reading, audiovisual speech analysis, and human-robot interaction, particularly in challenging environments characterized by low illumination or high dynamic range. Event-based lip reading, speaker recognition, and voice activity detection, however, mostly operate on a cropped region of interest (ROI), by hand or by the dataset, and no event-based method supplies that ROI as a spatial region; existing event-based face analysis gives the mouth as landmarks, which presents a mismatch between application and localization. The present work predicts a dense heatmap over the lip region from the full event "frame". Events are encoded as a polarity-separated voxel grid and processed at every location by a two-pathway continuous-time recurrent network (CT-RNN) with learned, log-space bounded time constants acting on the real elapsed time of each bin: a stateless fast pathway and a stateful slow pathway, utilised for refining and anchoring the prediction. The model reaches 69.5% on lips on four unseen speakers and switches target only 2.1 times per second, against 8.9 and 11.0 for convolutional baselines with more parameters. Adding a spatial encoder improves precision but fails on a new face scale. On a real event sensor, trained only on simulated events, the proposed model reaches 58.0% on lips against 43.2% for the CNN, with fewer than half its target switches.

authors.name: Hamze Hammami, Omar Eldardeer, Francesco Rea

papers.title: Auditing a Learned Simulator for Legged Robots: The Robotic World Model on ANYmal D
papers.summary: A legged robot can learn to walk inside a learned simulator: a neural network that predicts the robot's next state and is run forward on its own predictions. They are usually trained and checked one step ahead, although a policy uses them for a hundred steps or more. We audit one published system end to end, without a GPU: the dynamics model of the Robotic World Model (RWM) for the ANYmal D quadruped, and the uncertainty estimate of its follow-up, RWM-U. We rebuilt the model to match the released code's outputs, losses and gradients exactly, measured 101 trained simulators, 200 compressed copies and 38 simulators of three other architectures, and trained policies inside simulators that we tested in a hand-built MuJoCo model of the robot. Training on the model's own rollouts beat one-step training at 368 steps on all ten held-out episodes (registered), although one-step training was better one step ahead. One-step checks therefore misjudge design choices: pruning 30% of the weights kept 90% of the model's skill one step ahead and 39% at 2 s. Ensemble disagreement ranked rollout error well (Spearman +0.90 at 100 steps), yet covered 4.6% of outcomes at one sigma, against 68% for a calibrated estimate, as each network's own variance collapses under the implemented loss. Two checks that need no recorded future ranked some pools of simulators well, but neither was shown better than 8-step error in a primary test. At the robot level, accuracy has not predicted walking: all 18 fine-tuned copies we tested predicted better than the released model one and eight steps ahead, yet 13 gave failing policies, and registered tests of whether any check ranks simulators by their policies were not settled. In a secondary test, running the authors' policy inside each simulator ranked them well. We also report nine of our own claims that we withdrew. Scope: one robot, one gait, simulated data, no hardware.

authors.name: Joyjeet Singh

papers.title: Which Past Matters? Training History and Multi-Forecast Horizon in Equity Transformers
papers.summary: More historical data can improve estimation while introducing relationships that transfer poorly to current market conditions. We therefore examine how training quantity and historical selection interact with forecast horizon in intraday equity prediction. We deploy twelve configurations which combine four sampling and validation policies with 6, 12 and 24 month training quantities under a fixed cross-sectional Transformer and feature set. A monthly walk-forward experiment produces 264 refits and eight cumulative return forecasts from 5 to 120 minutes. Evaluation covers January 2025 through 20 October 2026 and uses cross-sectional Spearman information coefficients against future five-factor residual returns. Six-month recency sampling leads individual models at 5-15 minutes, while multi recency configurations lead at 20-30 minutes and uniform configurations at 60-120 minutes. Increasing training quantity does not uniformly improve accuracy while an equal-weight ensemble of all twelve models exceeds every individual mean at 15, 20 and 25 minutes, but not at the remaining horizons. These findings support evaluating historical selection jointly with forecast horizon without identifying a universal policy or a causal benefit from recency.

authors.name: Chariton Chalvatzis

papers.title: Capability Composition in Heterogeneous Teams via Barrier-Guided Diffusion Sampling
papers.summary: The agents in a heterogeneous team can cooperate to accomplish tasks that exceed their individual capabilities. The team trajectories for a cooperative task can be generated by a generative model, provided that the model has been trained on demonstrations of the agents cooperating. Yet, demonstrations of cooperation are costly and may not exist for tasks that the team has never performed. The conditions under which the agents can combine their capabilities, however, are physical properties of the team and are known before any demonstration is collected. We encode the conditions as constraints on the team trajectories, and we enforce the constraints while sampling from generative models trained on demonstrations of each agent alone. We prove that the proposed method can generate every team trajectory that satisfies the constraints, although the demonstrations contain no cooperation. Hence the constraints determine which team trajectories can be generated, and the demonstrations determine how likely each team trajectory is. Numerical results on two cooperative tasks show the effectiveness of the method, which generates cooperative team trajectories that satisfy the constraints and requires no retraining when agents join or leave the team. Finally, we implement the method on a multi-robot testbed.

authors.name: Diana Laura Morales, Ruoyu Lin, Magnus Egerstedt, Fabio Pasqualetti

papers.title: MoE--LoRA Methods for Multilingual Adaptation: A Systematic Empirical Study
papers.summary: Routed low-rank adapters offer a parameter-efficient means to improve the performance of large language models (LLMs) across tasks. Hence, it is assumed that they can also be used to improve the support of low-resource languages in LLMs, which currently serve English far better than the thousands of other languages spoken worldwide. However, this assumption has never been verified empirically under a shared multilingual evaluation protocol. We address exactly this gap by comparing eight low-rank adaptation (LoRA) methods on a frozen base model using 200 unique languages in more than 9{,}000 evaluation settings. Our results suggest that a reduced-scale search can identify viable configurations of LoRA methods but does not reliably predict their relative performance, as the top-ranking configuration is never best at scale. LoRA reliably improves language-model fit on translation data, consistently degrades reading comprehension, and benefits low-resource languages most. These findings suggest that LoRA methods should be regarded as targeted tools rather than general-purpose means for improving the multilingual capabilities of LLMs.

authors.name: Nikit Srivastava, Joel Dag, Ren\'e Speck, Axel-Cyrille Ngonga Ngomo

papers.title: D\'ej\`a View: A Shared Working-Memory Model for Visual Tasks
papers.summary: A working-memory model must remember stimuli and use its memory flexibly to perform different tasks. Here we introduce a model of working memory for images that combines dynamic activity with temporary associations between image features. We train the model on five tasks, including remembering a sample while other images are presented, categorizing distractor images while remembering the sample, and determining whether an image is new or has been presented before. The same trained model performs all tasks, guided by explicit cues about which response is required. We use this flexible memory model to ask how delay, distraction, and image history affect performance. Delays have little effect on sample-memory performance for the delays we tested, while seeing more images leads to more false alarms even when the target image appeared equally recently in all cases. On the sample-memory-plus-categorization task, the probability of correct responses on all questions decreases as more questions are asked, despite robust sample-memory performance. Finally, the model maintains stable performance across 40 brief trials of each task under the tested conditions. Together, these results demonstrate how a single working-memory system can be flexibly used to perform different tasks, and how its errors depend on both previous images and task demands.

authors.name: Mranmay Shetty, Gabriel Kreiman

papers.title: Multimodal Masked Diffusion Autoencoder for Modeling Impaired Driving
papers.summary: Human cognitive state (e.g., distraction, stress), gaze, and behavior interact with the driving environment in subtle ways that AI could use to assist drivers, but ground-truth labels for human cognitive state levels are costly to obtain at scale. We propose a multimodal masked-diffusion autoencoder, ID-MAE, that adds a self-supervised objective to impairment prediction: alongside predicting the impairment label as a masked token, it reconstructs masked gaze and trajectory. To probe the effects of different modalities and types of impairments on model inference, we introduce DIVERT, a driving-simulator dataset containing 103 hours of driving data (n = 109) with ten impairment inductions spanning cognitive, visual, and emotional states, recorded with gaze, vehicle state, and scene video. We demonstrate how ID-MAE affords significant improvements in impairment inference results on both the DIVERT dataset and existing datasets, and enables strong results in additional tasks, such as trajectory and gaze prediction. For location-matched pairs, our model achieves a paired AUC of 0.706 for impairment detection on DIVERT, compared to 0.590 without reconstruction loss, improving over existing baselines. We probe the design space in terms of input modalities, masking scheme, positional encoding, attention mechanism, and decoding. We also investigate the interaction between various impairments in training and inference, demonstrating that visually demanding distractions are separable from cognitive distractions. Code and data will be available upon acceptance.

authors.name: John Gideon, Anshul Gupta, Megan Applegate-Kenton, Kayli Battel, Todd J Rowell, Patricio Reyes Gomez, Laporsha Dees, Emily Sumner, Avinash Balachandran, Guy Rosman

papers.title: What Does a Bias Head Measure? Non-Identifiability in Head-Level Bias Attribution
papers.summary: Methods that localise social bias in large language models to individual attention heads and remove it by ablation are validated by their effect on a fairness metric, never by evidence that the statistic selecting the heads measures bias. We audit this on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The head map correlates at $\rho = -0.950$ and $-0.768$ with a label-blind response-length map, apparently identifying a surface confound. An intervention that breaks the length-label coupling rejects this reading: with the prompt held fixed, response length explains 1% of the statistic's variance. What does explain it is prompt identity, at 64% of variance, in an ordering that is not monotonic in length. Within any fixed prompt the fairness label, response length and the presence of a protected-group token are collinear at $\phi = 0.95$, partly by definition of the labelling rule, so no observational analysis can attribute the map to any of them, and no method in this family performs an experiment that could. The substantive claims fail independently: bias selectivity is not late-layer-concentrated on either model under either reference reading, and no head set we tested reduces the unfairness rate when ablated. Its complement, scored on the opposite label, reliably destroys refusal behaviour ($p = 2.7\times10^{-5}$), demonstrating that the pipeline detects effects at this scale.

authors.name: S. M Seefat Alam

papers.title: An inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient method for constrained convex finite-sum optimization
papers.summary: In this paper, we study a class of constrained convex finite-sum optimization problems. In many practical applications, all or some of the constraints are hard constraints that represent imperative requirements. Consequently, any desirable approximate solution must (nearly) satisfy these constraints. Motivated by this, we focus on computing an $\epsilon$-$surely\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ ($\epsilon$-SFSO) solution, in which the constraint violation is deterministically bounded by $\epsilon$, and the expected optimality gap is at most $\epsilon$. While a recently proposed stochastic variance-reduced first-order penalty method can compute an $\epsilon$-SFSO solution, there remains a significant gap between its first-order oracle complexity for computing an $\epsilon$-SFSO solution and that for computing an $\epsilon$-$expected\ feasible\ stochastic\ optimal$ solution, where both the expected constraint violation and the expected optimality gap are bounded by $\epsilon$. To narrow this gap, we propose an inexact stochastic variance-reduced gradient (SVRG) method that significantly improves the previously best-known first-order oracle complexity for computing an $\epsilon$-SFSO solution. Furthermore, when the objective consists of a single function, the proposed method reduces to a novel deterministic first-order method for solving standard convex conic optimization. It achieves a significantly lower gradient evaluation complexity with respect to the objective function compared to existing methods, and can outperform them when computing constraint gradients and projections onto the associated cone is cheaper than evaluating the objective gradient. Preliminary numerical results are presented to illustrate the performance of the proposed method.

authors.name: Zhaosong Lu, Yifeng Xiao

papers.title: Spool: Low-Latency Streaming Inference for Hybrid Vision-Language Models
papers.summary: Applications such as visual accessibility agents and robotics require answering questions about recent video content promptly, over a bounded window of past frames (e.g., the last two minutes). Hybrid vision-language models (VLMs), which interleave attention with linear recurrent layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), are attractive for this setting, but maintaining a sliding window is expensive. The reason is that recurrent layers combine all past frames into a shared state, so expiring old frames normally requires re-running the entire window through the model. We observe that the recurrent update is affine in the state with input-dependent coefficients, so the effect of each frame can be captured as a transformation that composes associatively. We present Spool, a training-free framework that caches per-frame state transformations and composes them efficiently as the window advances, removing expired frames from each recurrent layer's state without replaying frames through the backbone. Removal is exact within each layer; as with key-value eviction in attention, expired frames can retain residual influence through the cached inputs computed by earlier layers. We design a dedicated data structure and GPU kernels to achieve low caching and composition overhead. Across five open-source hybrid VLMs and four video reasoning benchmarks, Spool achieves the lowest p95 time-to-first-token in all 20 model-benchmark tests, reducing it by a geometric mean of $6.6\times$ over the faster of two recent vLLM baselines, while improving accuracy by 2.3 percentage points on average.

authors.name: Rui Ning, Om Chabra, Hari Balakrishnan

papers.title: Algorithmic Insurance
papers.summary: When artificial intelligence (AI) systems make errors in high-stakes domains such as medical diagnosis or autonomous driving, a single algorithmic flaw across varying contexts can generate heterogeneous losses that challenge traditional insurance assumptions. Algorithmic insurance, financial coverage for AI-induced damages, is an emerging market, yet insurers struggle to price these risks and AI developers lack frameworks linking system design to liability exposure. We connect a key operational choice in binary classification, how practitioners set decision thresholds, to tail risk exposure. Using conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) to capture extreme losses, we prove that established approaches such as accuracy maximization can significantly increase worst-case losses relative to tail risk optimization, with penalties growing at least quadratically as thresholds deviate from optimal. We propose a liability insurance contract that mandates risk-aware thresholds and characterize when it creates value for AI providers, extending the analysis to degrading model performance and human oversight. In a mammography case study, accuracy-maximizing thresholds carry up to four times the tail risk of CVaR-optimal thresholds. Insurance contracts create 7-8% gains for well-calibrated firms through risk transfer and regulatory capital relief, and up to 105% for poorly calibrated firms through mandatory recalibration, while partially aligned firms can lose under a strict mandate, calling for threshold flexibility in contract design. Unlike traditional insurance that merely transfers risk, algorithmic insurance can act as both a financial instrument and an operational governance mechanism, enabling risk transfer while improving AI safety.

authors.name: Dimitris Bertsimas, Agni Orfanoudaki

papers.title: Optimizer's Information Criterion: Dissecting and Correcting Bias in Data-Driven Optimization
papers.summary: In data-driven optimization, the sample performance of the obtained decision typically incurs an optimistic bias against the true performance, a phenomenon commonly known as the Optimizer's Curse and intimately related to overfitting in machine learning. We develop a general approach that we call \emph{Optimizer's Information Criterion (OIC)} to correct this bias. OIC generalizes the celebrated Akaike Information Criterion from the evaluation of model adequacy, used primarily for model selection, to objective performance in data-driven optimization, which is used for decision selection. Our approach analytically approximates and cancels out the bias that comprises the interplay between model fitting and downstream optimization. As such, it saves the computational need to repeatedly solve optimization problems in cross-validation, while operating more generally than other bias approximating scheme. We apply OIC to a range of data-driven optimization formulations comprising empirical and parametric models, their regularized counterparts, and furthermore contextual optimization. Finally, we provide numerical validation of the superior performance of our approach under synthetic and real-world datasets.

authors.name: Garud Iyengar, Henry Lam, Tianyu Wang

papers.title: Exact Sequence Interpolation with Transformers
papers.summary: We prove that transformers can exactly interpolate datasets of finite input sequences in $\mathbb{R}^d$, $d\geq 2$, with corresponding output sequences of smaller or equal length. Specifically, given $N$ sequences of arbitrary but finite lengths in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and output sequences of lengths $m^1, \dots, m^N \in \mathbb{N}$, we construct a transformer with $\mathcal{O}(\sum_{j=1}^N m^j)$ blocks and $\smash{\mathcal{O}(d \sum_{j=1}^N m^j)}$ parameters that exactly interpolates the dataset. Our construction provides complexity estimates that are independent of the input sequence length, by alternating feed-forward and self-attention layers and by capitalizing on the clustering effect inherent to the latter. Our novel constructive method also uses low-rank parameter matrices in the self-attention mechanism, a common feature of practical transformer implementations. These results are first established in the hardmax self-attention setting, where the geometric structure permits an explicit and quantitative analysis, and are then extended to the softmax setting. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of our exact interpolation construction to learning problems, in particular by providing convergence guarantees to a global minimizer under regularized training strategies. Our analysis contributes to the theoretical understanding of transformer models, offering an explanation for their excellent performance in exact sequence-to-sequence interpolation tasks.

authors.name: Albert Alcalde, Giovanni Fantuzzi, Enrique Zuazua

papers.title: SiGMA: Learning under Graph-Level Heterogeneity with Gated Message-Passing and Attention
papers.summary: In graph-level learning, graph neural networks are typically applied with a fixed computational template: the same depth, local message-passing operator, and global attention mechanism are used for every input graph. However, different graphs within the same dataset can vary substantially in prediction difficulty and may require different mixtures of local and non-local computation. We study this phenomenon as graph-level heterogeneity in both classification and regression tasks. To address it, we propose SiGMA (Sigmoid Gated Message-Passing and Attention), a gated hybrid graph neural network architecture that combines message-passing and attention heads within each layer. Inspired by the growing use of gated attention and gated computation in large language models and vision transformers, each head in SiGMA is modulated by a learned node-wise sigmoid gate, allowing the model to adaptively regulate which local or global mechanisms are active for different nodes, layers, and input graphs. The resulting architecture can emulate expressive message-passing backbones, admits near-identity computation paths that are not forced to over-smooth, and enables direct non-local communication beyond message-passing neighborhoods to mitigate over-squashing. Empirically, SiGMA achieves strong performance across graph-level benchmarks, consistently matching or improving over competitive graph transformer and hybrid baselines. Our results suggest that adapting computation to graph-level heterogeneity is a promising direction for building more flexible and effective graph learning architectures.

authors.name: Raphael Pellegrin, Lukas Fesser, Melanie Weber

papers.title: HOPSE: Scalable Higher-Order Positional and Structural Encoder for Combinatorial Representations
papers.summary: While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have proven highly effective at modeling relational data, pairwise connections cannot fully capture multi-way relationships naturally present in complex real-world systems. In response to this, Topological Deep Learning (TDL) leverages more general combinatorial representations--such as simplicial or cellular complexes--to accommodate higher-order interactions. Existing TDL methods often extend GNNs through Higher-Order Message Passing (HOMP), but face critical scalability challenges due to the steep complexity overhead of propagating messages through combinatorial structures. To overcome this limitation, we propose HOPSE (Higher-Order Positional and Structural Encoder), a framework free of learnable message passing layers that uses Hasse graph decompositions to derive efficient and expressive encodings over arbitrary higher-order domains. Notably, HOPSE training and inference scale linearly with the size of combinatorial representations while preserving the expressive power and permutation equivariance of the HOMP approaches. Experiments on molecular and topological benchmarks show that it matches or surpasses state-of-the-art performance while consistently achieving speedups over HOMP-based models, opening a new path for scalable TDL. The code is available at https://github.com/geometric-intelligence/topobench.

authors.name: Guillermo Bern\'ardez, Marco Montagna, Louis Van Langendonck, Martin Carrasco, Amirreza Akbari, Louisa Cornelis, Mathilde Papillon, Pere Barlet-Ros, Nina Miolane, Lev Telyatnikov

papers.title: Learning Greens Operators through Hierarchical Neural Networks Inspired by the Fast Multipole Method
papers.summary: The Fast Multipole Method (FMM) is an efficient numerical algorithm for computation of long-ranged forces in $N$-body problems within gravitational and electrostatic fields. This method utilizes multipole expansions of the Green's function inherent to the underlying dynamical systems. Despite its widespread application in physics and engineering, the integration of FMM with modern machine learning architectures remains underexplored. In this work, we propose a novel neural network architecture, the Neural FMM, that integrates the information flow of the FMM into a hierarchical machine learning framework for learning the Green's operator of an Elliptic PDE. Our Neural FMM architecture leverages a hierarchical computation flow of the FMM method to split up the local and far-field interactions and efficiently learn their respective representations.

authors.name: Emilio McAllister Fognini, Marta M. Betcke, Ben T. Cox

papers.title: Interpret Policies in Deep Reinforcement Learning using SILVER with RL-Guided Labeling: A Model-level Approach to High-dimensional and Multi-action Environments
papers.summary: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) achieves remarkable performance but lacks interpretability, limiting trust in policy behavior. The existing SILVER framework (Li, Siddique, and Cao 2025) explains RL policy via Shapley-based regression but remains restricted to low-dimensional, binary-action domains. We propose SILVER with RL-guided labeling, an enhanced variant that extends SILVER to multi-action and high-dimensional environments by incorporating the RL policy's own action outputs into the boundary points identification. Our method first extracts compact feature representations from image observations, performs SHAP-based feature attribution, and then employs RL-guided labeling to generate behaviorally consistent boundary datasets. Surrogate models, such as decision trees and regression-based functions, are subsequently trained to interpret RL policy's decision structure. We evaluate the proposed framework on two Atari environments using three deep RL algorithms and conduct human-subject study to assess the clarity and trustworthiness of the derived interpretable policy. Results show that our approach maintains competitive task performance while substantially improving transparency and human understanding of agent behavior. This work advances explainable RL by transforming SILVER into a scalable and behavior-aware framework for interpreting deep RL agents in high-dimensional, multi-action settings.

authors.name: Yiyu Qian, Liyuan Zhao

papers.title: Functional Compression as Occam's Razor: Algebraic Complexity from Sensitivity Minimization
papers.summary: Discovering discrete algebraic structures from data is a fundamental challenge in machine learning. We ask how continuous learning objectives can favor functional compression---representing data through shared algebraic composition rather than low-rank representations. We analyze the global optima of a canonical factorization model for algebraic completion (recovering finite binary operations) that demonstrated a preference for group operations. We measure algebraic complexity by the infimum of parameter sensitivity under exact reconstruction. We establish a universal complexity floor, whose attainment forces geometric alignment and unitarity of the latent representations. At the floor, input representations compose into the corresponding output representations; their reuse across the operation table propagates these local identities to enforce a globally shared algebraic structure. If the floor is not attained, a positive gap separates it from the feasible infimum. For cancellative operations, floor attainment forces the model's latent representation to be an injective homomorphism, equivalent to the target being isotopic to a group. In this case, every global minimizer is equivalent to the underlying group's unitary left-regular representation, up to isotopy and unitary gauge, resolving the central conjecture of Huh (2025). For non-cancellative operations, floor attainment forces exact structural redundancies (identical rows or columns) and is equivalent to a unitary factorization of the target's row- and column-reduced table with orthonormal output matrices, yielding the fewest distinct input matrices compatible with exact reconstruction. The resulting cancellative table then embeds in a group-isotope table. This analysis reveals a structural bias toward functional compression: at the sensitivity floor, algebraic composition of latent representations implements the target operation.

authors.name: Dongsung Huh, Lior Horesh, Halyun Jeong

papers.title: Agentic AI-Empowered Dynamic Survey Framework
papers.summary: Survey papers play a central role in synthesizing and organizing scientific knowledge, yet they are increasingly strained by the rapid growth of research output. As new work continues to appear after publication, surveys quickly become outdated, contributing to redundancy and fragmentation in the literature. We reframe survey writing as a long-horizon maintenance problem rather than a one-time generation task, treating surveys as living documents that evolve alongside the research they describe. We propose an agentic Dynamic Survey Framework that supports the continuous updating of existing survey papers by incrementally integrating new work while preserving survey structure and minimizing unnecessary disruption. Using a retrospective experimental setup, we demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively identifies and incorporates emerging research while preserving the coherence and structure of existing surveys, even over extended sequences of updates.

authors.name: Furkan Mumcu, Lokman Bekit, Michael J. Jones, Anoop Cherian, Yasin Yilmaz

papers.title: Beyond Success Rates: Trainability and Extractability for Offline GCRL
papers.summary: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL) methods are typically benchmarked by the success rates of optimized hyperparameter configurations. However, success rate by itself does not provide information about the sensitivity of algorithms to hyperparameters for value learning or policy extraction, since an algorithm could obtain the same success rate across a wide range of hyperparameters, or might succeed only on specific settings. We study this phenomenon in the offline GCRL algorithms GCIQL, GCIVL, QRL, and CRL under a shared policy extractor, by constructing landscapes of interaction between the learning rate and policy extraction hyperparameters such as the temperature of advantage-weighted regression (AWR). These landscapes reveal large, task-dependent differences in hyperparameter sensitivity. On AntMaze-M, 59% of QRL configurations and 66% of CRL configurations achieve at least 90% of the method's best sampled success rate, compared with 3% for both GCIQL and GCIVL. On Cube and Scene, GCIQL and GCIVL instead attain higher success over broader hyperparameter regions than QRL and CRL. To interpret these differences, we analyze how reliably learned advantages rank actual goals from the same trajectory above random goals, and how strongly AWR concentrates policy updates on a small subset of transitions. Our findings indicate strongly differing behavior of these algorithms at policy-extraction time, even under the same success rates. Given these results, we argue that offline GCRL methods should be evaluated by both attainable success and the needed hyperparameter range to sustain it, complemented by post-hoc diagnostics to understand the signal used to train the policy. The overview and code are available at https://luh-ai.github.io/GCRL-Landscapes/ .

authors.name: Jan Malte T\"opperwien, Aditya Mohan, Marius Lindauer

papers.title: Time-Delayed Transformers for Data-Driven Modeling of Low-Dimensional Dynamics
papers.summary: We propose the time-delayed transformer (TD-TF), a simplified transformer architecture for data-driven modeling of unsteady spatio-temporal dynamics. TD-TF bridges linear operator-based methods and deep sequence models by showing that a single-layer, single-head transformer can be interpreted as a nonlinear generalization of time-delayed dynamic mode decomposition (TD-DMD). The architecture is deliberately minimal, consisting of one self-attention layer with a single query per prediction and one feedforward layer, resulting in linear computational complexity in sequence length and a small parameter count. Numerical experiments demonstrate that TD-TF matches the performance of strong linear baselines on near-linear systems, while significantly outperforming them in nonlinear and chaotic regimes, where it accurately captures long-term dynamics. Validation studies on synthetic signals, unsteady aerodynamics, the Lorenz '63 system, and a reaction-diffusion model show that TD-TF preserves the interpretability and efficiency of linear models while providing substantially enhanced expressive power for complex dynamics.

authors.name: Albert Alcalde, Markus Widhalm, Emre Y{\i}lmaz

papers.title: GPTZero: Robust Detection of LLM-Generated Texts
papers.summary: While historical considerations surrounding text authenticity revolved primarily around plagiarism, the advent of large language models (LLMs) has introduced a new challenge: distinguishing human-authored from AI-generated text. This shift raises significant concerns, including the undermining of skill evaluations, the mass-production of low-quality content, and the proliferation of misinformation. Addressing these issues, we introduce GPTZero 5.0, a state-of-the-art industrial AI detection solution, offering reliable discernment between human and LLM-generated text. Our key contributions include: introducing a hierarchical, multi-task architecture enabling a flexible taxonomy of human and AI texts, setting a new state-of-the-art for AI detection accuracy on 11 independent third-party benchmarks and 18 writing domains, and achieving superior robustness to adversarial attacks and paraphrasing via multi-tiered automated red teaming. GPTZero offers accurate and explainable detection, and educates users on its responsible use, ensuring fair and transparent assessment of text.

authors.name: George Alexandru Adam, Alexander Cui, Edwin Thomas, Emily Napier, Nazar Shmatko, Yue Gao, Zikun Chen, Jacob Schnell, Jacob Junqi Tian, Alekhya Dronavalli, Edward Tian, Dongwon Lee

papers.title: Differentially Private Non-convex Distributionally Robust Optimization
papers.summary: Real-world deployments routinely face distribution shifts, group imbalances, and adversarial perturbations, under which the traditional Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) framework can degrade severely. Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) addresses this issue by optimizing the worst-case expected loss over an uncertainty set of distributions, offering a principled approach to robustness. Meanwhile, as training data in DRO always involves sensitive information, safeguarding it against leakage under Differential Privacy (DP) is essential. In contrast to classical DP-ERM, DP-DRO has received much less attention due to its minimax optimization structure with uncertainty constraint. To bridge the gap, we provide a comprehensive study of DP-(finite-sum)-DRO with $\psi$-divergence and non-convex loss. First, we study DRO with general $\psi$-divergence by reformulating it as a minimization problem, and develop a novel $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-DP optimization method, called DP Double-Spider, tailored to this structure. Under mild assumptions, we show that it achieves a utility bound of $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}+ (\frac{\sqrt{d \log (1/\delta)}}{n \varepsilon})^{2/3})$ in terms of the gradient norm, where $n$ denotes the data size and $d$ denotes the model dimension. We further improve the utility rate for specific divergences. In particular, for DP-DRO with KL-divergence, by transforming the problem into a compositional finite-sum optimization problem, we develop a DP Recursive-Spider method and show that it achieves a utility bound of $\mathcal{O}((\frac{\sqrt{d \log(1/\delta)}}{n\varepsilon})^{2/3} )$, matching the best-known result for non-convex DP-ERM. Experimentally, we demonstrate that our proposed methods outperform existing approaches for DP minimax optimization.

authors.name: Difei Xu, Meng Ding, Zebin Ma, Huanyi Xie, Youming Tao, Aicha Slaitane, Di Wang

papers.title: Memorization capacity of deep ReLU neural networks characterized by width and depth
papers.summary: This paper studies the memorization capacity of deep neural networks with ReLU activation. Specifically, we investigate the minimal size of such networks to memorize any $N$ data points in the unit ball with pairwise separation distance $\delta$ and labels from a finite set of size $C$. Most prior studies characterize the memorization capacity by the number of parameters or neurons. We extend these results by constructing ReLU networks with adjustable width $W$ and depth $L$ satisfying $W^2L^2\log W=\mathcal{O}(N(\log(\delta^{-1})+\log C))$ that can memorize any such dataset. We also establish width-depth lower bounds that depend explicitly on $\delta$ and $C$ for networks capable of memorizing all such datasets. When $\log(\delta^{-1})\asymp\log N$, our construction achieves $W^2L^2\asymp N$ for suitable choices of width and depth. This order is optimal if $\log C\asymp\log N$, and optimal up to logarithmic factors if $\log C=o(\log N)$.

authors.name: Xin Yang, Yunfei Yang

papers.title: Gradient Manipulation in Distributed Stochastic Gradient Descent with Strategic Agents: Truthful Incentives with Convergence Guarantees
papers.summary: Distributed learning has gained significant attention due to its advantages in scalability, privacy, and fault tolerance.In this paradigm, multiple agents collaboratively train a global model by exchanging parameters only with their neighbors. However, a key vulnerability of existing distributed learning approaches is their implicit assumption that all agents behave honestly during gradient updates. In real-world scenarios, this assumption often breaks down, as selfish or strategic agents may be incentivized to manipulate gradients for personal gain, ultimately compromising the final learning outcome. In this work, we propose a fully distributed payment mechanism that, for the first time, guarantees both truthful behaviors and accurate convergence in distributed stochastic gradient descent. This represents a significant advancement, as it overcomes two major limitations of existing truthfulness mechanisms for collaborative learning:(1) reliance on a centralized server for payment collection, and (2) sacrificing convergence accuracy to guarantee truthfulness. In addition to characterizing the convergence rate under general convex and strongly convex conditions, we also prove that our approach guarantees the cumulative gain that an agent can obtain through strategic behavior remains finite, even as the number of iterations approaches infinity--a property unattainable by most existing truthfulness mechanisms. Our experimental results on standard machine learning tasks, evaluated on benchmark datasets, confirm the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

authors.name: Ziqin Chen, Yongqiang Wang

papers.title: Physics Informed Reinforcement Learning with Gibbs Priors for Topology Control in Power Grids
papers.summary: Topology control for power grid operation is a challenging sequential decision making problem because the action space grows combinatorially with the size of the grid and action evaluation through simulation is computationally expensive. We propose a physics-informed Reinforcement Learning framework that combines semi-Markov control with a Gibbs prior, that encodes the system's physics, over the action space. The decision is only taken when the grid enters a hazardous regime, while a graph neural network surrogate predicts the post action overload risk of feasible topology actions. These predictions are used to construct a physics-informed Gibbs prior that both selects a small state-dependent candidate set and reweights policy logits before action selection. In this way, our method reduces exploration difficulty and online simulation cost while preserving the flexibility of a learned policy. We evaluate the approach in three realistic benchmark environments of increasing difficulty. Across all settings, the proposed method achieves a strong balance between control quality and computational efficiency: it matches oracle-level performance while being approximately $6\times$ faster on the first benchmark, reaches $94.6\%$ of oracle reward with roughly $200\times$ lower decision time on the second one, and on the most challenging benchmark improves over a PPO baseline by up to $255\%$ in reward and $284\%$ in survived steps while remaining about $2.5\times$ faster than a strong specialized engineering baseline. These results show that our method provides an effective mechanism for topology control in power grids.

authors.name: Pantelis Dogoulis, Maxime Cordy

papers.title: Untrained CNNs Exceed Backpropagation in V1 Alignment at High Evaluation Resolution: A Systematic RSA Comparison of Four Learning Rules Against Human fMRI
papers.summary: Revision note: the V1 result reported here is not robust to the analysis choices examined in arXiv:2611.15533; see page 1. We compare four learning rules (backpropagation (BP), feedback alignment (FA), predictive coding (PC), and spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP)) in identical convolutional networks against human fMRI from THINGS-fMRI (720 stimuli, 3 subjects) using representational similarity analysis (RSA), together with an untrained random-weights baseline that isolates the contribution of architecture. Models are trained on 32 px CIFAR-10 and evaluated at 224 px; results are averaged across 5 seeds, with uncertainty from resampling stimuli. At V1, the untrained baseline exceeds BP rho = 0.053$ vs. $0.022$; rho = +0.031$, 95% CI $[0.019, 0.043]$), and the same holds at V2. This advantage depends on the evaluation resolution: in the 5-seed model set of the resolution study (gap $+0.030$ at 224 px), it vanishes when the models are evaluated at their 32 px training resolution rho = -0.001, 95% CI $[-0.011, 0.009]$; arXiv:2608.12408). At LOC, BP, PC and STDP exceed the untrained baseline, FA is borderline, and the trained rules do not differ from each other. At IT, no two conditions can be distinguished at the low reliability of the data (leave-one-subject-out lower bound 0.021). FA has the lowest alignment at V1. At V1, an untrained network thus matches BP at the training resolution and exceeds it at 224 px; learning-rule differences are resolvable only at an intermediate area.

authors.name: Nils Leutenegger

papers.title: Transferable SCF-Acceleration through Solver-Aligned Initialization Learning
papers.summary: The cost of Kohn-Sham density functional theory (KS-DFT) calculations scales with the number of required solver iterations, which depend on the quality of the initial guess. Machine learning methods that predict initial guesses from molecular geometry can reduce this cost, but matrix-prediction models fail when extrapolating to larger molecules, degrading rather than accelerating convergence [Liu et al., 2025]. We show that this failure is a supervision problem, not an extrapolation problem: models trained on ground-state targets fit those targets well out of distribution, yet produce initial guesses that slow convergence. Solver-Aligned Initialization Learning (SAIL) resolves this for both Hamiltonian and density matrix models by differentiating through parts of the self-consistent field (SCF) solver end-to-end. We introduce the Effective Relative Iteration Count (ERIC), a correction to the commonly used RIC that accounts for hidden Fock-build overhead. On QM40, which contains molecules up to 4$\times$ larger than the training distribution, SAIL reduces ERIC by 40% (PBE), 35% (SCAN), and 32% (B3LYP), more than doubling the previous state-of-the-art reduction on B3LYP. On QMugs molecules 10$\times$ larger than the training set, SAIL delivers a 1.35$\times$ wall-time speedup at the hybrid level of theory, extending ML SCF acceleration to large drug-like molecules.

authors.name: Eike S. Eberhard, Viktor Kotsev, Timm G\"uthle, Stephan G\"unnemann

papers.title: DiffATS: Diffusion in Aligned Tensor Space
papers.summary: Direct diffusion modeling of high-resolution spatiotemporal fields is computationally challenging. Parameter-efficient primitives address this by representing high-dimensional data with a compact set of parameters. In this paper, we construct data-dependent tensor primitives without pretrained compression autoencoders. Our construction starts from Tucker decomposition, which captures low-rank multilinear structure through a core tensor and mode-wise factors. However, Tucker factors are non-unique: the same tensor can be represented by different rotated factors, which complicates generative modeling. We address this issue with orthogonal Procrustes (OP) alignment. Specifically, we select medoid anchor matrices from the data and align the factor matrices to resolve the gauge ambiguity. This yields matrix Grassmannian primitives and tensor Grassmannian primitives that are compact, data-adaptive, and directly decodable by explicit multilinear reconstruction. Theoretically, we prove that the proposed primitive maps are homeomorphisms between low-rank tensors and their corresponding primitive spaces, certifying that the representations are non-degenerate and topologically faithful. Building on these primitives, we propose *Diffusion in Aligned Tensor Space* (DiffATS), a generative framework that trains diffusion models directly on aligned tensor primitives. Across images, videos, and PDE solutions, DiffATS achieves strong unconditional and conditional generation performance while compressing original data by $3.9\times$ to $210\times$, without relying on any pretrained deep compression autoencoders.

authors.name: Jinhua Lyu, Tianmin Yu, Brian Kim, Lizhuo Zhou, Chanwook Park, Naichen Shi

papers.title: When is Warmstarting Effective for Scaling Language Models?
papers.summary: Model growth from a given checkpoint aims to accelerate training of a larger model, offering potential resource savings. Despite recent interest, warmstarting has seen limited practical adoption in large-scale training. We attribute this to two underexplored factors: (1) an overemphasis on preserving the smaller model's performance at initialization, which constrains operator design for new architectures, and (2) insufficient analysis of how growth interacts with hyperparameters and scaling behavior, compounded by inconsistent growth factors across the literature. We show that preserving the base model's initial post-growth performance is not necessary for strong final performance, and that simple, architecture-agnostic growth strategies can outperform more complex warmstarting operators. Crucially, we empirically identify an upper bound on the growth factor $g$ beyond which training from scratch is more efficient. We observe this across multiple ablation setups. Notably, this limit is also present, but unreported, in prior published results. Across our experiments on dense MLPs and dense language models, we find that a $2\times$ growth factor is the most reliable in yielding convergence speedups, with gains most pronounced under 20 tokens/parameter budgets and diminishing as budget increases. We fit scaling laws over these observations to provide predictive guidance for practitioners deciding when and how much to grow. Together, our analysis provides practical guidelines and empirical limits for model growth.

authors.name: Neeratyoy Mallik, Maciej Janowski, Johannes Hog, Herilalaina Rakotoarison, Josif Grabocka, Frank Hutter, Aaron Klein

papers.title: Decision-Aware Proximal Bridge Learning for Optimal Treatment Selection
papers.summary: Individualized treatment selection with continuous actions requires accurate causal response estimation in decision-relevant regions, rather than uniformly over the entire action space. Estimating a global causal response surface and then choosing the treatment that maximizes it can therefore be suboptimal, since standard estimation objectives allocate modeling effort according to the observed treatment distribution rather than the regions that determine the optimal decision. While decision-aware approaches have been studied in unconfounded settings, this problem remains underexplored in proximal causal inference, where proxy variables and bridge functions enable identification under suitable assumptions even in the presence of hidden confounding. Despite recent progress, proximal methods have primarily focused on treatment-effect and potential-outcome estimation rather than treatment selection and optimal decision-making. To bridge this gap, we introduce a policy-targeted weighted bridge loss that emphasizes decision-relevant treatment regions while retaining global stabilization. We prove a regret bound showing that the proposed weighted bridge loss controls treatment-selection regret through a weighted ill-posedness constant. We instantiate the framework in decision-aware variants of several proximal bridge solvers, yielding practical algorithms that alternate between weighted bridge estimation, response-surface projection, policy update, and weight refinement. Empirically, we find that decision-aware weighting reduces regret across several bridge solvers, suggesting improved treatment selection in proximal settings.

authors.name: Tom\`as Garriga, Alejandro Almod\'ovar, Axel Brando, Gerard Sanz, Eduard Serrahima de Cambra, Juan Parras

papers.title: Q-LocalAdam: Memory-Efficient Client-Side Adaptive Optimization for Edge Federated Learning
papers.summary: On-device federated learning (FL) on edge devices is limited by the memory required by client-side adaptive optimizers. Maintaining optimizer states locally increases memory usage and can restrict the size of models that can be deployed on resource-constrained edge devices. State quantization can reduce this memory footprint, but uniform compression methods may perform poorly under skewed, non-IID data distributions because they can lose small-variance values that are important for stable optimization. We present \textbf{Q-LocalAdam}, a distribution-aware optimizer for memory-constrained edge devices. It applies block-wise linear quantization to the bounded momentum state and log-space quantization to the heavy-tailed variance state. A post-dequantization variance floor is used to maintain numerical stability. Q-LocalAdam reduces the persistent optimizer-state memory footprint while achieving convergence close to full-precision training. We evaluate Q-LocalAdam on physical edge devices and GPU, measuring persistent optimizer-state storage, process-level memory, and the latency introduced by quantization across human activity, vision, and language workloads. Our results show reduced peak resident memory with modest latency overhead, indicating that distribution-aware state compression can make adaptive optimization practical for edge deployments.

authors.name: Vedant Waykole, Haroon R. Lone

papers.title: Beyond Single Slot: Joint Optimization for Multi-Slot Guaranteed Display Advertising
papers.summary: Guaranteed display advertising is crucial for platform monetization, yet existing methods often operate under a single-slot assumption, limiting their ability to optimize allocation across multi-slot page views. In this paper, we propose a novel joint optimization framework for multi-slot GD allocation, addressing key challenges such as slot-level redundancy, contract imbalance, and exposure concentration. Our approach formulates the allocation as an offline bipartite matching problem with a contract roulette mechanism for slot exclusivity and Page View constraints for impression control, and incorporates a scalable allocation optimization algorithm for efficient large-scale deployment. Extensive online tests on the Meituan advertising platform demonstrate that our method significantly improves merchant ROI, platform revenue efficiency, and contract fulfillment robustness. Specifically, online A/B tests show a 28.99% increase in Average Revenue Per User under 70% traffic, and DID analysis further indicates improved contract stability, demonstrating the strong applicability and effectiveness of our framework in real-world advertising deployments.

authors.name: Zhaoqi Zhang, Jiaming Deng, Miao Xie, Linyou Cai, Qianlong Xie, Xingxing Wang, Siqiang Luo, Gao Cong

papers.title: Cross-Species RSA Reveals Conserved Early Visual Alignment but Divergent Higher-Area Rankings Across Human fMRI and Macaque Electrophysiology
papers.summary: CORRECTION (August 2026): an evaluation-mode defect in the shared feature-extraction pipeline affected the predictive-coding and STDP conditions. It applies to both sides of every comparison here: the human values are reprinted from the companion study and the macaque values use the same checkpoints. In a single-seed re-evaluation with repaired checkpoints, macaque STDP at V1 moves from 0.305 to 0.266 and PC from 0.210 to 0.178, level with the untrained baseline, so finding (2) holds for STDP but not for PC; the V4 and IT orderings change, while V2 is unchanged. Revision note: the human V1 results are not robust to the analysis choices examined in arXiv:2611.15533. Findings (1), (3) and (4) are unaffected, and other conditions change by at most 0.0034. Five-seed analysis, tau, noise ceilings and stimulus control not re-computed. See the correction note on page 1; the abstract below is unchanged. Follow-up study: arXiv:2608.12408. Does the relationship between learning rules and brain alignment generalize across species? We test the same five learning rules against macaque electrophysiology. The macaque data come from MajajHong2015 (V4/IT, 3,200 presentations, 88/168 neurons) and FreemanZiemba2013 (V1/V2, 135 stimuli, 102/103 neurons). Using RSA with identical model weights from our human study, we find: (1) all models achieve higher alignment with macaque early visual cortex (rho = 0.15-0.30 at V1/V2) than with human fMRI (rho = 0.01-0.08); (2) STDP and PC produce the highest macaque V1/V2 alignment; (3) at IT, rankings show no detectable correlation across species (Kendall's tau = 0.00), though this null is expected given that n = 5 provides power only at tau = +/-1.0; (4) a pretrained ResNet-50 achieves rho = 0.25 at macaque IT, substantially above all custom CNN conditions (rho = 0.07-0.14), suggesting IT alignment is limited by model capacity rather than by the learning rule.

authors.name: Nils Leutenegger

papers.title: RelPrism: Multi-Faceted Self-Supervised Learning on Relational Databases
papers.summary: Relational databases (RDBs) remain the backbone of modern data systems and support a broad spectrum of predictive tasks that require multi-faceted information from different perspectives and granularities. For example, user churn prediction is often formulated as a binary classification task that relies more on user interaction patterns reflecting activity levels, whereas consumption value estimation is a fine-grained regression task that may require composite evidence from both user attributes and user--item interaction behaviors. Therefore, a central challenge is to learn representations with comprehensive coverage of the information underlying RDB tasks. A natural solution is to leverage self-supervised learning (SSL) for pre-training. However, existing SSL methods typically derive supervision from a single facet, such as node-level intrinsic attributes or subgraph-level relational structures. Consequently, their pre-training objectives provide limited support for adaptation. To this end, we propose RelPrism, a multi-faceted self-supervised learning framework for RDBs. Concretely, RelPrism first constructs intrinsic, relational, and hybrid attributes from distinct perspectives. It then applies multi-granularity clustering to each attribute perspective to form corresponding pseudo-task pools. Pre-training over these task pools exposes representations to comprehensive attribute perspectives and granularity levels, providing a stronger basis for downstream adaptation. Extensive experiments on 14 tasks across 5 real-world datasets show that RelPrism improves ROC-AUC by 4.15% on classification tasks and reduces MAE by 10.75% on regression tasks over state-of-the-art baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/RelPrism.

authors.name: Jinyu Yang, Cheng Yang, Junze Chen, Zedi Liu, Muhan Zhang, Hanyang Peng, Chuan Shi

papers.title: An Open-Source Training Dataset for Foundation Models for Hyperparameter Optimization
papers.summary: Most hyperparameter optimization methods require extensive tuning of their own hyperparameters, often limiting their ability to generalize across different benchmark families. Foundation models for hyperparameter optimization that learn optimization principles from a large collection of optimization trajectories offer a promising alternative, with the potential to outperform manually designed methods across diverse problem classes. However, prior work as either relied on non-public datasets or on purely synthetic data, limiting reproducibility and generalization to real-world problems. As a result, progress in this area has been constrained by the lack of large-scale, real-world, publicly available pre-training data. We introduce BBO-Pile, the first open-source dataset comprising over 500K optimization trajectories evaluated across 3,095 different hyperparameter optimization tasks and global optimization problems for different optimizers, which represents by far the largest public dataset for this task. Using this dataset, we train a family of foundation models at multiple scales, ranging from 2M to 80M parameters and from 200M to 2B training tokens, and study their scaling behavior with respect to compute. Our results demonstrate that large-scale pre-training is a viable and effective approach to imitate hyperparameter optimization methods, paving the way for future research in this direction.

authors.name: Aaron Klein, Herilalaina Rakotoarison, Luca Thale-Bombien, David Salinas

papers.title: Supervised Training Rapidly Degrades Early Visual Cortex Alignment Across Biologically Plausible Learning Rules
papers.summary: CORRECTION (August 2026): the central finding of this paper is not supported. An evaluation-mode defect left the batch-normalisation layers of the predictive-coding and STDP conditions in training mode during feature extraction, producing their apparent preservation of V1 alignment. With the defect repaired, predictive coding degrades V1 alignment more than backpropagation does, not less. The finding that training degrades V1 alignment for every rule tested does survive. [Revision note: not robust to the analysis choices examined in arXiv:2611.15533.] See the correction note on page 1; the original abstract below and the body are unchanged from v1. Corrected analysis: arXiv:2608.12408. Revision note: see Comments. Random, untrained neural networks consistently match or exceed trained networks in representational similarity to early visual cortex. This puzzling finding challenges the assumption that learning improves brain alignment. We investigate it by tracking representational similarity analysis (RSA) alignment to human fMRI data across training for four learning rules: backpropagation (BP), feedback alignment (FA), predictive coding (PC), and spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP). Using 720 object images from the THINGS database and fMRI data from three subjects across six visual ROIs, we measure Spearman correlations between model and brain representational dissimilarity matrices at eight training checkpoints (epochs 0-40). We find that (1) a single epoch of training reduces V1 alignment by 25-90%, depending on the learning rule; (2) backpropagation reduces V1 alignment most severely (delta r = -0.080), while predictive coding and STDP preserve substantially more (delta r ~ -0.04); and (3) a weaker, opposite tendency appears in object-selective cortex (LOC), where BP shows the largest increase in alignment during training, although the absolute change is small.

authors.name: Nils Leutenegger

papers.title: Multivariate Distributional Reinforcement Learning Using Sliced Divergences
papers.summary: Distributional reinforcement learning (DRL) models the full return distribution rather than expectations, but extending it to multivariate settings remains challenging. Many common metrics do not naturally generalize beyond one dimension or lose computational tractability, and the multivariate case introduces additional difficulties such as general matrix discounting, for which no contraction results are available. We introduce Sliced Distributional Reinforcement Learning (SDRL), which lifts tractable one-dimensional divergences to multivariate return distributions via projections. We prove Bellman contraction for uniform slicing under shared scalar discounting, and introduce a maximum-slicing variant with contraction under general dense discount matrices. SDRL supports a broad class of base divergences; we analyze Wasserstein, Cram\'er, and Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), and characterize which SDRL variants suit the standard single-sample Bellman update used in distributional RL. We evaluate SDRL on a toy chain problem and a gridworld image-based environment as well as a subset of Atari games.

authors.name: Baptiste Debes, Tinne Tuytelaars

papers.title: Semi-Supervised Learning with Noisy Proxy Covariates: Generalization Bounds and Distribution Regression
papers.summary: In many modern machine learning pipelines, abundant pretrained representations serve as noisy proxy covariates, while task-specific labels remain scarce.
